1	# Proof of P2
2	
3	All counting variables are positive integers, unless stated otherwise. We use
4	the definitions of \(Q,g,E,V_f\) in `problem.md` and assume P1 exactly as
5	supplied. In particular, \(g(q,l)\) is periodic in \(l\), is real, and is the
6	density of squarefree integers in the indicated residue class. Constants
7	introduced below depend only on \(f\), or on the displayed positive error
8	parameter, as indicated.
9	
10	**1. Polynomial weights and endpoints.** Put
11	
12	\[
13	\alpha=1-\frac1d.
14	\]
15	
16	There are constants \(0<A\le1\) and \(B\ge1\), depending only on \(f\), such
17	that, for every real \(t\ge1\),
18	
19	\[
20	 At^d\le f(t)\le Bt^d,\qquad
21	 1\le f'(t)\le Bt^{d-1}.                                      \tag{1}
22	\]
23	
24	For \(d\ge2\), enlarge \(B\) to ensure
25	
26	\[
27	 |f''(t)|\le Bt^{d-2}\quad(t\ge1).                            \tag{2}
28	\]
29	
30	These constants exist because the leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive,
31	\(f(t)/t^d\) is positive and continuous on \([1,\infty)\), and its limit at
32	infinity is positive. The upper bounds follow by bounding each coefficient
33	of the relevant polynomial. For \(d=1\), \(f''=0\).
34	
35	For the interval in the proposition, write
36	
37	\[
38	 W=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k),\qquad
39	 N=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor.
40	\]
41	
42	Thus this sum has exactly \(N\le y\) terms. Let \(n=\lfloor z\rfloor\) and
43	\(m=\lfloor y\rfloor\). For each of its \(N\) terms, the error on replacing
44	\(f'(k)\) by its integral over \([k-1,k]\) has absolute value at most
45	\(\int_{k-1}^k|f''(t)|\,dt\). After summing these \(N\) errors, their total
46	absolute value is at most \(\int_n^m|f''(t)|\,dt\). The two endpoint
47	integrals needed to replace \([n,m]\) by \([z,y]\) have lengths less than
48	one each. Consequently,
49	
50	\[
51	 \left|W-\int_z^y f'(t)\,dt\right|
52	 \le 2\sup_{1\le t\le y}f'(t)+\int_1^y|f''(t)|\,dt
53	 \le 3B y^{d-1}.                                             \tag{3}
54	\]
55	
56	For \(d\ge2\), the integral in this inequality is at most
57	\(B(y^{d-1}-1)/(d-1)\le By^{d-1}\). For \(d=1\), it is zero, so (3) holds
58	in that case as well. Since \(Y=f(y)\ge Ay^d\), the constant
59	
60	\[
61	 K=3BA^{-\alpha}
62	\]
63	
64	satisfies
65	
66	\[
67	 |W-(Y-Z)|\le K Y^\alpha,\qquad
68	 0\le W\le(1+K)Y.                                           \tag{4}
69	\]
70	
71	Here we used \(Y\ge2\) and \(Y^\alpha\le Y\).
72	
73	We shall also use the following elementary divisor bound. If \(\tau(q)\)
74	denotes the number of divisors of \(q\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is
75	a finite \(D_\eta\) such that
76	
77	\[
78	 \tau(q)\le D_\eta q^\eta\quad(q\ge1).                       \tag{5}
79	\]
80	
81	Indeed, for primes \(p\ge2^{1/\eta}\) and integers \(e\ge0\),
82	\(e+1\le2^e\le p^{\eta e}\). For each of the finitely many smaller primes,
83	\(\sup_{e\ge0}(e+1)p^{-\eta e}\) is finite. Their product gives \(D_\eta\).
84	
85	**2. An elementary mixed-moment estimate.** For a positive integer \(a\),
86	define
87	
88	\[
89	 N_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\a\mid n}}\mu^2(n),\qquad
90	 D_a=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\mu(r)}{[a,r^2]},
91	\]
92	
93	where brackets denote the least common multiple. The series for \(D_a\)
94	converges absolutely because \([a,r^2]\ge r^2\). The elementary identity
95	\(\mu^2(n)=\sum_{r^2\mid n}\mu(r)\) gives
96	
97	\[
98	 N_a(x)=\sum_{r\le\sqrt x}\mu(r)
99	              \left\lfloor\frac{x}{[a,r^2]}\right\rfloor.
100	\]
101	
102	This \(r\)-sum has \(\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor\) terms. Each floor replacement
103	has error of absolute value at most one; their total error is at most
104	\(\sqrt x\). The omitted part of the absolutely convergent main-term series
105	has absolute value at most
106	
107	\[
108	 x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{[a,r^2]}
109	 \le x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{r^2}
110	 \le\frac{x}{\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor}
111	 \le2\sqrt x.
112	\]
113	
114	Thus, uniformly in \(a\ge1\) and real \(x\ge2\),
115	
116	\[
117	 |N_a(x)-xD_a|\le3\sqrt x.                                  \tag{6}
118	\]
119	
120	Fix a positive integer \(q\), and put
121	
122	\[
123	 q_1=\prod_{p\parallel q}p,\qquad
124	 A_q=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1},\qquad
125	 H(q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)^2.
126	\]
127	
128	By the absolutely convergent Euler product for \(\zeta(2)\),
129	\(cA_q\le1\). For squarefree \(n\), the zero-density exception in P1 never
130	occurs, since no prime square divides \(n\). Expanding the remaining factors
131	in P1 therefore gives the exact identity
132	
133	\[
134	 \mu^2(n)g(q,n)
135	 =\frac{cA_q}{q}\mu^2(n)
136	       \sum_{\substack{a\mid q_1\\a\mid n}}\frac{\mu(a)}a.
137	                                                                    \tag{7}
138	\]
139	
140	Set
141	
142	\[
143	 B(q)=\frac{cA_q}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac{\mu(a)}aD_a.
144	\]
145	
146	The divisor sum here has \(\tau(q_1)\le\tau(q)\) terms. Before summing, the
147	error contributed by a divisor \(a\), on using (6) in (7), has absolute
148	value at most \(3cA_q\sqrt x/(qa)\). After summing over these divisors,
149	
150	\[
151	 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xB(q)\right|
152	 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac1a
153	 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{8}
154	\]
155	
156	There is no uniform-limit issue in identifying \(B(q)\). For this fixed
157	\(q\), periodicity gives a sum of exactly \(q\) residue classes,
158	
159	\[
160	 \sum_{n\le t}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)
161	 =\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)Q(t;q,l).
162	\]
163	
164	Divide by \(t\) and let \(t\to\infty\). By the definition of the densities,
165	the right side tends to \(H(q)\); by (8), the left side tends to \(B(q)\).
166	Hence \(B(q)=H(q)\). In particular, if
167	
168	\[
169	 M(x;q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)E(x;q,l),
170	\]
171	
172	then (8) proves the uniform estimate
173	
174	\[
175	 |M(x;q)|
176	 =\left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xH(q)\right|
177	 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{9}
178	\]
179	
180	Taking \(a=1\) in (6), the Euler product
181	\(D_1=\sum_{r\ge1}\mu(r)/r^2=c\) also gives
182	
183	\[
184	 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right|\le3\sqrt x.           \tag{10}
185	\]
186	
187	**3. Exact expansion and its accumulated errors.** For every integer
188	\(1\le q\le x\), counting ordered pairs of squarefree integers in the same
189	residue class gives
190	
191	\[
192	 \sum_{l=1}^q Q(x;q,l)^2
193	 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
194	     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq).                         \tag{11}
195	\]
196	
197	Indeed, pairs with equal coordinates contribute the first term. For a pair
198	with unequal coordinates, its positive difference is exactly \(hq\) for
199	one of the \(\lfloor x/q\rfloor\) possible positive integers \(h\). The
200	number of such pairs in increasing order is \(C_x(hq)\), and reversing
201	their order gives the factor two. These are exact finite identities,
202	including for nonintegral \(x\).
203	
204	Since \(Q=E+xg\), expansion of the square, followed by the definition of
205	\(M(x;q)\), gives
206	
207	\[
208	 \sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
209	 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
210	     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq)
211	     -x^2H(q)-2xM(x;q).                                     \tag{12}
212	\]
213	
214	Sum this identity over the \(N\) integers \(z<k\le y\), with \(q=f(k)\)
215	and weight \(f'(k)\). The hypotheses imply \(q\le Y\le x\). There is no
216	approximation in the correlation sum or in the term containing \(H(q)\).
217	Thus the difference asserted in the first part of P2 is exactly
218	
219	\[
220	 R=\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W
221	      +cx\bigl(W-(Y-Z)\bigr)
222	      -2x\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k)).                     \tag{13}
223	\]
224	
225	We bound each of these three errors. Before summing the diagonal error
226	over \(k\), its absolute value is at most \(3\sqrt x f'(k)\), by (10).
227	After summing its \(N\) terms, (4) gives
228	
229	\[
230	 \left|\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W\right|
231	 \le3\sqrt x W
232	 \le3(1+K)\sqrt x Y
233	 \le3(1+K)x^{3/2}.                                          \tag{14}
234	\]
235	
236	The endpoint error in (13) satisfies
237	
238	\[
239	 |cx(W-(Y-Z))|\le cKxY^\alpha.                              \tag{15}
240	\]
241	
242	For the mixed error, fix the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) and set
243	\(\eta=\varepsilon/2\). Before summing over \(k\), (1), (5), (9), and
244	\(f(k)\le x\) give
245	
246	\[
247	 |f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
248	 \le3D_\eta x^{1/2+\eta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
249	 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}\frac{x^{1/2+\eta}}{k}.              \tag{16}
250	\]
251	
252	There are \(N\le\lfloor y\rfloor\le A^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) terms. Summing
253	the displayed reciprocal bound, rather than its maximum, yields
254	
255	\[
256	 \sum_{z<k\le y}|f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
257	 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}x^{1/2+\eta}(1+\log y).              \tag{17}
258	\]
259	
260	For completeness, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor y\rfloor}1/k\le1+\log y\)
261	follows by bounding the terms with \(k\ge2\) by
262	\(\int_{k-1}^{k}dt/t\). From \(Ay^d\le x\),
263	
264	\[
265	 1+\log y\le L\log(2x),\qquad
266	 L=1+\frac1d+\frac{\log(A^{-1})}{d}.
267	\]
268	
269	The elementary maximum of \(u e^{-\eta u}\), for \(u\ge0\), gives
270	
271	\[
272	 \log(2x)\le J_\eta x^\eta,\qquad
273	 J_\eta=\log2+\frac1{e\eta}\quad(x\ge2).
274	\]
275	
276	Consequently, with \(M_{f,\varepsilon}=3D_\eta BLJ_\eta/A\), the error
277	before multiplication by \(2x\) in (13) is at most
278	\(M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1/2+2\eta}\). After that multiplication it is at
279	most
280	
281	\[
282	 2x\left|\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k))\right|
283	 \le2M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/2+\varepsilon}.                   \tag{18}
284	\]
285	
286	Combining (13)--(18), and using \(x^{3/2}\le x^{3/2+\varepsilon}\), proves
287	
288	\[
289	 \left|V_f(x;z,y)
290	  -\{cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)\}\right|
291	 \le\bigl(3(1+K)+2M_{f,\varepsilon}\bigr)x^{3/2+\varepsilon}
292	       +cKxY^{1-1/d}.                                      \tag{19}
293	\]
294	
295	This also covers \(z=y\), and intervals containing no integer \(k\).
296	
297	**4. The published full-variance bound, with its normalization checked.**
298	We use J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D.
299	Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers* (1998),
300	*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A* **356**,
301	739--761, [DOI:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183).
302	The reference is the supplied `papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf`, Lemma 2.2, on page
303	6 of that PDF. Its statement, quoted verbatim with its mathematical
304	notation typeset in LaTeX, is:
305	
306	> **Lemma 2.2.** Suppose that \(Q\) and \(x\) are positive real numbers,
307	> and that \(k\) is an integer with \(k\ge2\). Then for each positive
308	> number \(\varepsilon\),
309	> \[
310	> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)\ll
311	> \begin{cases}
312	> x^{2/k+\varepsilon}Q^{2-2/k},&\text{when }1\le Q\le x,\\
313	> Q^2\log(2Q),&\text{when }Q>x.
314	> \end{cases}
315	> \]
316	
317	The source's defining equations (2.6) and (2.7), also quoted, are
318	
319	> \[
320	> \sum_{\substack{1\le n\le x\\n\equiv a\pmod q}}\mu_k(n)
321	> =\frac{x}{\zeta(k)}g_k(q,(q,a))+E_k(x;q,a),                 \tag{2.6}
322	> \]
323	> \[
324	> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q
325	>                          |E_k(x;q,a)|^2.                  \tag{2.7}
326	> \]
327	
328	Here \(\mu_k\) is the source's characteristic function of the \(k\)-free
329	integers; its \(k\) is the power parameter, independent of our polynomial
330	index. In particular, \(\mu_2=\mu^2\).
331	
332	We check the density normalization without assuming any formula for the
333	source's \(g_k\). Fix positive integers \(q,a\), with \(1\le a\le q\), and
334	apply the quoted lemma with power parameter \(k=2\), \(Q=q\), error
335	parameter \(1/2\), and real \(t\ge\max\{2,q\}\) in place of \(x\).
336	These are positive real \(Q,t\), an integer power parameter at least two,
337	a positive error parameter, and \(1\le Q\le t\), as required. Since each
338	term of (2.7) is nonnegative, the lemma implies, for a constant \(B_{1/2}\),
339	
340	\[
341	 |E_2(t;q,a)|^2\le B_{1/2}t^{3/2}q,\qquad
342	 \frac{|E_2(t;q,a)|}{t}
343	       \le B_{1/2}^{1/2}q^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0.
344	\]
345	
346	Dividing (2.6) by \(t\) therefore shows that
347	
348	\[
349	 c\,g_2(q,(q,a))
350	 =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{Q(t;q,a)}t=g(q,a).
351	\]
352	
353	Thus \(E_2(x;q,a)=E(x;q,a)\) exactly, and the source's sum (2.7) is
354	
355	\[
356	 U(x,Q):=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q E(x;q,a)^2.
357	\]
358	
359	The inner sum includes every residue class, including the classes not
360	coprime to \(q\); there is no missing coprimality restriction. With power
361	parameter \(2\), the exponents in the lemma's first branch are
362	
363	\[
364	 \frac22+\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon,\qquad
365	 2-\frac22=1.
366	\]
367	
368	It follows that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(B_\varepsilon\)
369	such that
370	
371	\[
372	 U(x,Q)\le B_\varepsilon x^{1+\varepsilon}Q
373	       \qquad(1\le Q\le x).                                \tag{20}
374	\]
375	
376	The statement was checked both in the text extraction and in a rendered
377	image of the relevant supplied PDF page.
378	
379	**5. Disposal of the initial moduli.** Let \(z\ge1\) be real, set
380	\(Z=f(z)\le x\), and use the definition \(V_f(x,z)\) in `problem.md`.
381	For each of the \(\lfloor z\rfloor\) indices in this sum, (1) gives the
382	weight bound
383	
384	\[
385	 0<f'(k)\le Bz^{d-1}\le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha.                \tag{21}
386	\]
387	
388	Moreover, \(f'(t)\ge1\) implies
389	\(f(k+1)-f(k)=\int_k^{k+1}f'(t)\,dt\ge1\). Hence the integers \(f(k)\)
390	are distinct positive moduli, and all those with \(k\le z\) are at most
391	\(Z\). Each residue-class variance is nonnegative. Before summing in \(k\),
392	(21) bounds its weighted value by \(BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha\) times the
393	corresponding unweighted variance. After summing its \(\lfloor z\rfloor\)
394	terms and enlarging to the \(\lfloor Z\rfloor\) possible positive moduli,
395	we obtain
396	
397	\[
398	 0\le V_f(x,z)
399	 \le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha
400	       \sum_{1\le q\le Z}\sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
401	 =BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha U(x,Z).                              \tag{22}
402	\]
403	
404	To apply (20) here, \(x\ge2\) is positive, \(Q=Z=f(z)\ge2\) is a
405	positive real number, \(1\le Q\le x\) is part of the present hypotheses,
406	the power parameter is the integer \(2\ge2\), and the error parameter is
407	the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). These check every hypothesis of the
408	quoted lemma for this application. Equations (20) and (22) yield
409	
410	\[
411	 0\le V_f(x,z)
412	 \le BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
413	       x^{1+\varepsilon}Z^{1+\alpha}
414	 =BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
415	       x^{1+\varepsilon}f(z)^{2-1/d}.                        \tag{23}
416	\]
417	
418	Taking a common constant larger than the constants in (19) and (23)
419	proves both assertions of P2, uniformly in all the stated ranges.
420	
421	**Source and verification notes.** R. C. Vaughan, *A variance for k-free
422	numbers in arithmetic progressions* (2005), *Proceedings of the London
423	Mathematical Society* (3) **91**, 573--597,
424	[DOI:10.1112/S0024611505015352](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024611505015352),
425	was consulted as a bibliographical pointer to the 1998 lemma. The estimate
426	used in the proof is the verbatim lemma quoted above from the supplied
427	1998 paper. A bibliographical web search returned post-2010 sources;
428	reading stopped when their dates were identified, and their content was
429	excluded from the argument.
430	
431	A Python sanity check tested (9) and the exact identity (12) for all
432	integers \(1\le q\le\lfloor x\rfloor\), with
433	\(x\in\{2,3.25,10,31.75,100,200.5\}\), comprising 346 pairs \((x,q)\).
434	It used direct squarefree counts and the density formula of P1. Identity
435	(12) agreed within floating-point tolerance, and every test satisfied
436	(9). These computations serve only as checks; the proofs of (9) and
437	(12) are the finite identities and inequalities above.

# Proof of P2

All counting variables are positive integers, unless stated otherwise. We use
the definitions of \(Q,g,E,V_f\) in `problem.md` and assume P1 exactly as
supplied. In particular, \(g(q,l)\) is periodic in \(l\), is real, and is the
density of squarefree integers in the indicated residue class. Constants
introduced below depend only on \(f\), or on the displayed positive error
parameter, as indicated.

**1. Polynomial weights and endpoints.** Put

\[
\alpha=1-\frac1d.
\]

There are constants \(0<A\le1\) and \(B\ge1\), depending only on \(f\), such
that, for every real \(t\ge1\),

\[
 At^d\le f(t)\le Bt^d,\qquad
 1\le f'(t)\le Bt^{d-1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), enlarge \(B\) to ensure

\[
 |f''(t)|\le Bt^{d-2}\quad(t\ge1).                            \tag{2}
\]

These constants exist because the leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive,
\(f(t)/t^d\) is positive and continuous on \([1,\infty)\), and its limit at
infinity is positive. The upper bounds follow by bounding each coefficient
of the relevant polynomial. For \(d=1\), \(f''=0\).

For the interval in the proposition, write

\[
 W=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k),\qquad
 N=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor.
\]

Thus this sum has exactly \(N\le y\) terms. Let \(n=\lfloor z\rfloor\) and
\(m=\lfloor y\rfloor\). For each of its \(N\) terms, the error on replacing
\(f'(k)\) by its integral over \([k-1,k]\) has absolute value at most
\(\int_{k-1}^k|f''(t)|\,dt\). After summing these \(N\) errors, their total
absolute value is at most \(\int_n^m|f''(t)|\,dt\). The two endpoint
integrals needed to replace \([n,m]\) by \([z,y]\) have lengths less than
one each. Consequently,

\[
 \left|W-\int_z^y f'(t)\,dt\right|
 \le 2\sup_{1\le t\le y}f'(t)+\int_1^y|f''(t)|\,dt
 \le 3B y^{d-1}.                                             \tag{3}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), the integral in this inequality is at most
\(B(y^{d-1}-1)/(d-1)\le By^{d-1}\). For \(d=1\), it is zero, so (3) holds
in that case as well. Since \(Y=f(y)\ge Ay^d\), the constant

\[
 K=3BA^{-\alpha}
\]

satisfies

\[
 |W-(Y-Z)|\le K Y^\alpha,\qquad
 0\le W\le(1+K)Y.                                           \tag{4}
\]

Here we used \(Y\ge2\) and \(Y^\alpha\le Y\).

We shall also use the following elementary divisor bound. If \(\tau(q)\)
denotes the number of divisors of \(q\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is
a finite \(D_\eta\) such that

\[
 \tau(q)\le D_\eta q^\eta\quad(q\ge1).                       \tag{5}
\]

Indeed, for primes \(p\ge2^{1/\eta}\) and integers \(e\ge0\),
\(e+1\le2^e\le p^{\eta e}\). For each of the finitely many smaller primes,
\(\sup_{e\ge0}(e+1)p^{-\eta e}\) is finite. Their product gives \(D_\eta\).

**2. An elementary mixed-moment estimate.** For a positive integer \(a\),
define

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\a\mid n}}\mu^2(n),\qquad
 D_a=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\mu(r)}{[a,r^2]},
\]

where brackets denote the least common multiple. The series for \(D_a\)
converges absolutely because \([a,r^2]\ge r^2\). The elementary identity
\(\mu^2(n)=\sum_{r^2\mid n}\mu(r)\) gives

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{r\le\sqrt x}\mu(r)
              \left\lfloor\frac{x}{[a,r^2]}\right\rfloor.
\]

This \(r\)-sum has \(\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor\) terms. Each floor replacement
has error of absolute value at most one; their total error is at most
\(\sqrt x\). The omitted part of the absolutely convergent main-term series
has absolute value at most

\[
 x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{[a,r^2]}
 \le x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{r^2}
 \le\frac{x}{\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor}
 \le2\sqrt x.
\]

Thus, uniformly in \(a\ge1\) and real \(x\ge2\),

\[
 |N_a(x)-xD_a|\le3\sqrt x.                                  \tag{6}
\]

Fix a positive integer \(q\), and put

\[
 q_1=\prod_{p\parallel q}p,\qquad
 A_q=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1},\qquad
 H(q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)^2.
\]

By the absolutely convergent Euler product for \(\zeta(2)\),
\(cA_q\le1\). For squarefree \(n\), the zero-density exception in P1 never
occurs, since no prime square divides \(n\). Expanding the remaining factors
in P1 therefore gives the exact identity

\[
 \mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\frac{cA_q}{q}\mu^2(n)
       \sum_{\substack{a\mid q_1\\a\mid n}}\frac{\mu(a)}a.
                                                                    \tag{7}
\]

Set

\[
 B(q)=\frac{cA_q}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac{\mu(a)}aD_a.
\]

The divisor sum here has \(\tau(q_1)\le\tau(q)\) terms. Before summing, the
error contributed by a divisor \(a\), on using (6) in (7), has absolute
value at most \(3cA_q\sqrt x/(qa)\). After summing over these divisors,

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xB(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac1a
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{8}
\]

There is no uniform-limit issue in identifying \(B(q)\). For this fixed
\(q\), periodicity gives a sum of exactly \(q\) residue classes,

\[
 \sum_{n\le t}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)Q(t;q,l).
\]

Divide by \(t\) and let \(t\to\infty\). By the definition of the densities,
the right side tends to \(H(q)\); by (8), the left side tends to \(B(q)\).
Hence \(B(q)=H(q)\). In particular, if

\[
 M(x;q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)E(x;q,l),
\]

then (8) proves the uniform estimate

\[
 |M(x;q)|
 =\left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xH(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{9}
\]

Taking \(a=1\) in (6), the Euler product
\(D_1=\sum_{r\ge1}\mu(r)/r^2=c\) also gives

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right|\le3\sqrt x.           \tag{10}
\]

**3. Exact expansion and its accumulated errors.** For every integer
\(1\le q\le x\), counting ordered pairs of squarefree integers in the same
residue class gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q Q(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq).                         \tag{11}
\]

Indeed, pairs with equal coordinates contribute the first term. For a pair
with unequal coordinates, its positive difference is exactly \(hq\) for
one of the \(\lfloor x/q\rfloor\) possible positive integers \(h\). The
number of such pairs in increasing order is \(C_x(hq)\), and reversing
their order gives the factor two. These are exact finite identities,
including for nonintegral \(x\).

Since \(Q=E+xg\), expansion of the square, followed by the definition of
\(M(x;q)\), gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq)
     -x^2H(q)-2xM(x;q).                                     \tag{12}
\]

Sum this identity over the \(N\) integers \(z<k\le y\), with \(q=f(k)\)
and weight \(f'(k)\). The hypotheses imply \(q\le Y\le x\). There is no
approximation in the correlation sum or in the term containing \(H(q)\).
Thus the difference asserted in the first part of P2 is exactly

\[
 R=\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W
      +cx\bigl(W-(Y-Z)\bigr)
      -2x\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k)).                     \tag{13}
\]

We bound each of these three errors. Before summing the diagonal error
over \(k\), its absolute value is at most \(3\sqrt x f'(k)\), by (10).
After summing its \(N\) terms, (4) gives

\[
 \left|\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W\right|
 \le3\sqrt x W
 \le3(1+K)\sqrt x Y
 \le3(1+K)x^{3/2}.                                          \tag{14}
\]

The endpoint error in (13) satisfies

\[
 |cx(W-(Y-Z))|\le cKxY^\alpha.                              \tag{15}
\]

For the mixed error, fix the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) and set
\(\eta=\varepsilon/2\). Before summing over \(k\), (1), (5), (9), and
\(f(k)\le x\) give

\[
 |f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le3D_\eta x^{1/2+\eta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}\frac{x^{1/2+\eta}}{k}.              \tag{16}
\]

There are \(N\le\lfloor y\rfloor\le A^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) terms. Summing
the displayed reciprocal bound, rather than its maximum, yields

\[
 \sum_{z<k\le y}|f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}x^{1/2+\eta}(1+\log y).              \tag{17}
\]

For completeness, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor y\rfloor}1/k\le1+\log y\)
follows by bounding the terms with \(k\ge2\) by
\(\int_{k-1}^{k}dt/t\). From \(Ay^d\le x\),

\[
 1+\log y\le L\log(2x),\qquad
 L=1+\frac1d+\frac{\log(A^{-1})}{d}.
\]

The elementary maximum of \(u e^{-\eta u}\), for \(u\ge0\), gives

\[
 \log(2x)\le J_\eta x^\eta,\qquad
 J_\eta=\log2+\frac1{e\eta}\quad(x\ge2).
\]

Consequently, with \(M_{f,\varepsilon}=3D_\eta BLJ_\eta/A\), the error
before multiplication by \(2x\) in (13) is at most
\(M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1/2+2\eta}\). After that multiplication it is at
most

\[
 2x\left|\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k))\right|
 \le2M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/2+\varepsilon}.                   \tag{18}
\]

Combining (13)--(18), and using \(x^{3/2}\le x^{3/2+\varepsilon}\), proves

\[
 \left|V_f(x;z,y)
  -\{cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)\}\right|
 \le\bigl(3(1+K)+2M_{f,\varepsilon}\bigr)x^{3/2+\varepsilon}
       +cKxY^{1-1/d}.                                      \tag{19}
\]

This also covers \(z=y\), and intervals containing no integer \(k\).

**4. The published full-variance bound, with its normalization checked.**
We use J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D.
Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers* (1998),
*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A* **356**,
739--761, [DOI:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183).
The reference is the supplied `papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf`, Lemma 2.2, on page
6 of that PDF. Its statement, quoted verbatim with its mathematical
notation typeset in LaTeX, is:

> **Lemma 2.2.** Suppose that \(Q\) and \(x\) are positive real numbers,
> and that \(k\) is an integer with \(k\ge2\). Then for each positive
> number \(\varepsilon\),
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)\ll
> \begin{cases}
> x^{2/k+\varepsilon}Q^{2-2/k},&\text{when }1\le Q\le x,\\
> Q^2\log(2Q),&\text{when }Q>x.
> \end{cases}
> \]

The source's defining equations (2.6) and (2.7), also quoted, are

> \[
> \sum_{\substack{1\le n\le x\\n\equiv a\pmod q}}\mu_k(n)
> =\frac{x}{\zeta(k)}g_k(q,(q,a))+E_k(x;q,a),                 \tag{2.6}
> \]
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q
>                          |E_k(x;q,a)|^2.                  \tag{2.7}
> \]

Here \(\mu_k\) is the source's characteristic function of the \(k\)-free
integers; its \(k\) is the power parameter, independent of our polynomial
index. In particular, \(\mu_2=\mu^2\).

We check the density normalization without assuming any formula for the
source's \(g_k\). Fix positive integers \(q,a\), with \(1\le a\le q\), and
apply the quoted lemma with power parameter \(k=2\), \(Q=q\), error
parameter \(1/2\), and real \(t\ge\max\{2,q\}\) in place of \(x\).
These are positive real \(Q,t\), an integer power parameter at least two,
a positive error parameter, and \(1\le Q\le t\), as required. Since each
term of (2.7) is nonnegative, the lemma implies, for a constant \(B_{1/2}\),

\[
 |E_2(t;q,a)|^2\le B_{1/2}t^{3/2}q,\qquad
 \frac{|E_2(t;q,a)|}{t}
       \le B_{1/2}^{1/2}q^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0.
\]

Dividing (2.6) by \(t\) therefore shows that

\[
 c\,g_2(q,(q,a))
 =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{Q(t;q,a)}t=g(q,a).
\]

Thus \(E_2(x;q,a)=E(x;q,a)\) exactly, and the source's sum (2.7) is

\[
 U(x,Q):=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q E(x;q,a)^2.
\]

The inner sum includes every residue class, including the classes not
coprime to \(q\); there is no missing coprimality restriction. With power
parameter \(2\), the exponents in the lemma's first branch are

\[
 \frac22+\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon,\qquad
 2-\frac22=1.
\]

It follows that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(B_\varepsilon\)
such that

\[
 U(x,Q)\le B_\varepsilon x^{1+\varepsilon}Q
       \qquad(1\le Q\le x).                                \tag{20}
\]

The statement was checked both in the text extraction and in a rendered
image of the relevant supplied PDF page.

**5. Disposal of the initial moduli.** Let \(z\ge1\) be real, set
\(Z=f(z)\le x\), and use the definition \(V_f(x,z)\) in `problem.md`.
For each of the \(\lfloor z\rfloor\) indices in this sum, (1) gives the
weight bound

\[
 0<f'(k)\le Bz^{d-1}\le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha.                \tag{21}
\]

Moreover, \(f'(t)\ge1\) implies
\(f(k+1)-f(k)=\int_k^{k+1}f'(t)\,dt\ge1\). Hence the integers \(f(k)\)
are distinct positive moduli, and all those with \(k\le z\) are at most
\(Z\). Each residue-class variance is nonnegative. Before summing in \(k\),
(21) bounds its weighted value by \(BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha\) times the
corresponding unweighted variance. After summing its \(\lfloor z\rfloor\)
terms and enlarging to the \(\lfloor Z\rfloor\) possible positive moduli,
we obtain

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha
       \sum_{1\le q\le Z}\sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha U(x,Z).                              \tag{22}
\]

To apply (20) here, \(x\ge2\) is positive, \(Q=Z=f(z)\ge2\) is a
positive real number, \(1\le Q\le x\) is part of the present hypotheses,
the power parameter is the integer \(2\ge2\), and the error parameter is
the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). These check every hypothesis of the
quoted lemma for this application. Equations (20) and (22) yield

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}Z^{1+\alpha}
 =BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}f(z)^{2-1/d}.                        \tag{23}
\]

Taking a common constant larger than the constants in (19) and (23)
proves both assertions of P2, uniformly in all the stated ranges.

**Source and verification notes.** R. C. Vaughan, *A variance for k-free
numbers in arithmetic progressions* (2005), *Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society* (3) **91**, 573--597,
[DOI:10.1112/S0024611505015352](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024611505015352),
was consulted as a bibliographical pointer to the 1998 lemma. The estimate
used in the proof is the verbatim lemma quoted above from the supplied
1998 paper. A bibliographical web search returned post-2010 sources;
reading stopped when their dates were identified, and their content was
excluded from the argument.

A Python sanity check tested (9) and the exact identity (12) for all
integers \(1\le q\le\lfloor x\rfloor\), with
\(x\in\{2,3.25,10,31.75,100,200.5\}\), comprising 346 pairs \((x,q)\).
It used direct squarefree counts and the density formula of P1. Identity
(12) agreed within floating-point tolerance, and every test satisfied
(9). These computations serve only as checks; the proofs of (9) and
(12) are the finite identities and inequalities above.

1	\chapter{Correlations of squarefree numbers}\label{ch:correlations}
2	
3	The off-diagonal term $S_f$ is a weighted sum of the correlations $C_x(m)$ of \eqref{eq:Cx}. We need an asymptotic formula for $C_x(m)$ that is uniform in the whole range $1\le m\le x$, including differences $m$ close to $x$, where the number $x-m$ of available pairs is small. Counts of pairs of squarefree numbers with a given difference have a long history (see for example \cite{mirsky1949}, and the discussion of the related binary additive problem in \cite[\S1]{bgpvw1998}). The archived proof gives a self-contained elementary argument with an explicit absolute constant. The archived plan anticipated a circle-method argument based on \cite{bgpvw1998}, but the proof does not need it. (Archived source: proposition P3.)
4	
5	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:corr}
6	There is an absolute constant $K_{\mathrm c}$ such that for all real $x\ge2$ and all integers $1\le m\le x$,
7	\[
8	\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\Sing(m)\bigr|\le K_{\mathrm c}\,x^{4/5}.
9	\]
10	One may take $K_{\mathrm c}=67+2D_{1/10}$, with $D_{1/10}$ as in \cref{lem:divisor}. In particular, for every $\eps>0$ the bound $C(\eps)x^{4/5+\eps}$ holds, which is the form recorded in the archived plan.
11	\end{proposition}
12	
13	\begin{proof}
14	Put $L=x-m\ge0$ and $H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor$, so that $\frac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}$ and $H\ge1$. All bounds below hold for every real $L\ge0$, including $L<1$, when $C_x(m)=0$.
15	
16	\emph{Truncation.} For $k\ge1$ split \eqref{eq:mu2} as $\mu^2(k)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)$, where
17	\[
18	T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e\le H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e),\qquad R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e>H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e).
19	\]
20	Then $|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k)$ and $|R_H(k)|\le\#\{e>H:e^2\mid k\}$. Each of the sets $\{n:1\le n\le L\}$ and $\{n+m:1\le n\le L\}$ consists of integers in $[1,x]$, because $m+L=x$. Each contains at most $x/e^2$ multiples of $e^2$. Therefore, by \cref{lem:sums}(a),
21	\begin{equation}\label{eq:RH-sum}
22	\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n)|\le\sum_{e>H}\frac x{e^2}\le\frac xH,\qquad\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n+m)|\le\frac xH.
23	\end{equation}
24	The exact identity
25	\[
26	\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
27	\]
28	together with $0\le\mu^2\le1$ and $|T_H(n)|\le\tau(n)\le D_{1/10}x^{1/10}$ (\cref{lem:divisor}) bounds each summand by $|R_H(n)|+D_{1/10}x^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|$. Summing with \eqref{eq:RH-sum},
29	\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-trunc}
30	\Bigl|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\Bigr|\le(1+D_{1/10}x^{1/10})\frac xH\le2x^{3/5}+2D_{1/10}x^{7/10}.
31	\end{equation}
32	
33	\emph{Counting the truncated congruences.} Let $e_1,e_2\le H$ and $g=(e_1,e_2)$. The congruences $n\equiv0\bmod e_1^2$ and $n\equiv-m\bmod e_2^2$ are soluble exactly when $g^2\mid m$. Necessity follows by reducing modulo $g^2$. For sufficiency write $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ with $(a,b)=1$ and $n=e_1^2u$; the second congruence becomes $a^2u\equiv-m/g^2\bmod b^2$, which determines $u$ modulo $b^2$. Hence the solutions form one residue class modulo $e_1^2e_2^2/g^2$. For any residue class modulo $h$ with representative $r$, the number of its members in $[1,L]$ is $\lfloor(L-r)/h\rfloor-\lfloor-r/h\rfloor=L/h+\theta$ with $|\theta|\le1$. Expanding both truncated sums therefore gives
34	\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-AH}
35	\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=L\,\mathcal A_H(m)+E_H,\qquad|E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5},
36	\end{equation}
37	where
38	\[
39	\mathcal A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{e_1,e_2\le H\\(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m}}\frac{\mu(e_1)\mu(e_2)(e_1,e_2)^2}{e_1^2e_2^2}.
40	\]
41	
42	\emph{Completing the series.} Let $\mathcal A(m)$ denote the same sum over all $e_1,e_2\ge1$. Writing $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ and dropping the coprimality of $a,b$ shows absolute convergence:
43	$\sum_{e_1,e_2}(e_1,e_2)^2/(e_1e_2)^2\le\sum_gg^{-2}\sum_aa^{-2}\sum_bb^{-2}\le8$. For the tail with $e_1>H$, the same substitution gives the bound $\sum_gg^{-2}\bigl(\sum_{a>H/g}a^{-2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_bb^{-2}\bigr)$. For $g\le H$ the summand is at most $g^{-2}(2g/H)\cdot2=4/(gH)$ by \cref{lem:sums}(a), and summing over $g\le H$ gives at most $4(1+\log H)/H$. For $g>H$ the summand is at most $4/g^2$, and these sum to at most $4/H$. By symmetry the tail with $e_2>H$ has the same bound, so
44	\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-tail}
45	|\mathcal A(m)-\mathcal A_H(m)|\le\frac{8(2+\log H)}H,
46	\end{equation}
47	uniformly in $m$, because the condition $(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m$ was dropped.
48	
49	\emph{The Euler product.} By absolute convergence, $\mathcal A(m)$ factors over primes, the argument of \cref{lem:euler} applying verbatim to the double sum. Only the exponents $0$ and $1$ occur in $e_1,e_2$. At a prime $p$ the four choices contribute $1$, $-p^{-2}$, $-p^{-2}$, and $p^{-2}\one_{p^2\mid m}$, so by \eqref{eq:sing}
50	\[
51	\mathcal A(m)=\prod_p\Bigl(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\one_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\Bigr)=\Sing(m).
52	\]
53	
54	\emph{Conclusion.} Since $0\le L\le x$, $H\ge\frac12x^{2/5}$ and $\log H\le\frac25\log x\le2x^{1/5}$ (\cref{lem:sums}(d)), \eqref{eq:corr-tail} gives
55	\[
56	L\,|\mathcal A_H(m)-\Sing(m)|\le16x^{3/5}\bigl(2+\tfrac25\log x\bigr)\le32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
57	\]
58	Combining with \eqref{eq:corr-trunc} and \eqref{eq:corr-AH} gives $|C_x(m)-L\Sing(m)|\le(2+2D_{1/10}+1+64)x^{4/5}$.
59	\end{proof}
60	
61	\begin{remark}
62	The constant $D_{1/10}$ is astronomically large, but only its existence matters. For the application in \cref{ch:assembly} only the exponent $4/5$ is relevant: summing the error over the roughly $x\log x$ weighted pairs $(h,k)$ costs $x^{9/5+\eps}$, and this caps the saving in \cref{thm:main} at $\eta_d\le1/5$.
63	\end{remark}

\chapter{Correlations of squarefree numbers}\label{ch:correlations}

The off-diagonal term $S_f$ is a weighted sum of the correlations $C_x(m)$ of \eqref{eq:Cx}. We need an asymptotic formula for $C_x(m)$ that is uniform in the whole range $1\le m\le x$, including differences $m$ close to $x$, where the number $x-m$ of available pairs is small. Counts of pairs of squarefree numbers with a given difference have a long history (see for example \cite{mirsky1949}, and the discussion of the related binary additive problem in \cite[\S1]{bgpvw1998}). The archived proof gives a self-contained elementary argument with an explicit absolute constant. The archived plan anticipated a circle-method argument based on \cite{bgpvw1998}, but the proof does not need it. (Archived source: proposition P3.)

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:corr}
There is an absolute constant $K_{\mathrm c}$ such that for all real $x\ge2$ and all integers $1\le m\le x$,
\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\Sing(m)\bigr|\le K_{\mathrm c}\,x^{4/5}.
\]
One may take $K_{\mathrm c}=67+2D_{1/10}$, with $D_{1/10}$ as in \cref{lem:divisor}. In particular, for every $\eps>0$ the bound $C(\eps)x^{4/5+\eps}$ holds, which is the form recorded in the archived plan.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $L=x-m\ge0$ and $H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor$, so that $\frac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}$ and $H\ge1$. All bounds below hold for every real $L\ge0$, including $L<1$, when $C_x(m)=0$.

\emph{Truncation.} For $k\ge1$ split \eqref{eq:mu2} as $\mu^2(k)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)$, where
\[
T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e\le H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e),\qquad R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e>H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e).
\]
Then $|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k)$ and $|R_H(k)|\le\#\{e>H:e^2\mid k\}$. Each of the sets $\{n:1\le n\le L\}$ and $\{n+m:1\le n\le L\}$ consists of integers in $[1,x]$, because $m+L=x$. Each contains at most $x/e^2$ multiples of $e^2$. Therefore, by \cref{lem:sums}(a),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RH-sum}
\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n)|\le\sum_{e>H}\frac x{e^2}\le\frac xH,\qquad\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n+m)|\le\frac xH.
\end{equation}
The exact identity
\[
\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
together with $0\le\mu^2\le1$ and $|T_H(n)|\le\tau(n)\le D_{1/10}x^{1/10}$ (\cref{lem:divisor}) bounds each summand by $|R_H(n)|+D_{1/10}x^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|$. Summing with \eqref{eq:RH-sum},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-trunc}
\Bigl|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\Bigr|\le(1+D_{1/10}x^{1/10})\frac xH\le2x^{3/5}+2D_{1/10}x^{7/10}.
\end{equation}

\emph{Counting the truncated congruences.} Let $e_1,e_2\le H$ and $g=(e_1,e_2)$. The congruences $n\equiv0\bmod e_1^2$ and $n\equiv-m\bmod e_2^2$ are soluble exactly when $g^2\mid m$. Necessity follows by reducing modulo $g^2$. For sufficiency write $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ with $(a,b)=1$ and $n=e_1^2u$; the second congruence becomes $a^2u\equiv-m/g^2\bmod b^2$, which determines $u$ modulo $b^2$. Hence the solutions form one residue class modulo $e_1^2e_2^2/g^2$. For any residue class modulo $h$ with representative $r$, the number of its members in $[1,L]$ is $\lfloor(L-r)/h\rfloor-\lfloor-r/h\rfloor=L/h+\theta$ with $|\theta|\le1$. Expanding both truncated sums therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-AH}
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=L\,\mathcal A_H(m)+E_H,\qquad|E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5},
\end{equation}
where
\[
\mathcal A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{e_1,e_2\le H\\(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m}}\frac{\mu(e_1)\mu(e_2)(e_1,e_2)^2}{e_1^2e_2^2}.
\]

\emph{Completing the series.} Let $\mathcal A(m)$ denote the same sum over all $e_1,e_2\ge1$. Writing $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ and dropping the coprimality of $a,b$ shows absolute convergence:
$\sum_{e_1,e_2}(e_1,e_2)^2/(e_1e_2)^2\le\sum_gg^{-2}\sum_aa^{-2}\sum_bb^{-2}\le8$. For the tail with $e_1>H$, the same substitution gives the bound $\sum_gg^{-2}\bigl(\sum_{a>H/g}a^{-2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_bb^{-2}\bigr)$. For $g\le H$ the summand is at most $g^{-2}(2g/H)\cdot2=4/(gH)$ by \cref{lem:sums}(a), and summing over $g\le H$ gives at most $4(1+\log H)/H$. For $g>H$ the summand is at most $4/g^2$, and these sum to at most $4/H$. By symmetry the tail with $e_2>H$ has the same bound, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-tail}
|\mathcal A(m)-\mathcal A_H(m)|\le\frac{8(2+\log H)}H,
\end{equation}
uniformly in $m$, because the condition $(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m$ was dropped.

\emph{The Euler product.} By absolute convergence, $\mathcal A(m)$ factors over primes, the argument of \cref{lem:euler} applying verbatim to the double sum. Only the exponents $0$ and $1$ occur in $e_1,e_2$. At a prime $p$ the four choices contribute $1$, $-p^{-2}$, $-p^{-2}$, and $p^{-2}\one_{p^2\mid m}$, so by \eqref{eq:sing}
\[
\mathcal A(m)=\prod_p\Bigl(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\one_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\Bigr)=\Sing(m).
\]

\emph{Conclusion.} Since $0\le L\le x$, $H\ge\frac12x^{2/5}$ and $\log H\le\frac25\log x\le2x^{1/5}$ (\cref{lem:sums}(d)), \eqref{eq:corr-tail} gives
\[
L\,|\mathcal A_H(m)-\Sing(m)|\le16x^{3/5}\bigl(2+\tfrac25\log x\bigr)\le32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\]
Combining with \eqref{eq:corr-trunc} and \eqref{eq:corr-AH} gives $|C_x(m)-L\Sing(m)|\le(2+2D_{1/10}+1+64)x^{4/5}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The constant $D_{1/10}$ is astronomically large, but only its existence matters. For the application in \cref{ch:assembly} only the exponent $4/5$ is relevant: summing the error over the roughly $x\log x$ weighted pairs $(h,k)$ costs $x^{9/5+\eps}$, and this caps the saving in \cref{thm:main} at $\eta_d\le1/5$.
\end{remark}

1	# Proof of P3
2	
3	We prove the stronger bound
4	\[
5	\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
6	\tag{1}
7	\]
8	with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
9	The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
10	No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
11	dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.
12	
13	## An explicit divisor bound
14	
15	Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
16	\(n\). Define the absolute constant
17	\[
18	D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
19	\]
20	where the product is over primes. We will use
21	\[
22	\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
23	\tag{2}
24	\]
25	Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
26	\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
27	then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
28	\[
29	(a+1)p^{-a/10}
30	\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
31	=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
32	\]
33	Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
34	(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
35	all at least one.
36	
37	We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
38	integers \(H\):
39	\[
40	\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
41	\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
42	\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
43	\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
44	\tag{3}
45	\]
46	The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
47	integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
48	Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).
49	
50	## Truncating the square-divisor identities
51	
52	Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
53	\[
54	L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
55	\]
56	In particular,
57	\[
58	\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
59	\tag{4}
60	\]
61	For positive integers \(k\), define
62	\[
63	T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
64	R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
65	\]
66	All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
67	\[
68	\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
69	\tag{5}
70	\]
71	follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
72	least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
73	Also
74	\[
75	|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
76	|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
77	\tag{6}
78	\]
79	
80	For either of the two sets
81	\[
82	I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
83	I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
84	\]
85	there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
86	For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
87	\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
88	\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
89	for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
90	\[
91	\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
92	\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
93	\le\frac{x}{H}.
94	\tag{7}
95	\]
96	This estimate also holds when either set is empty.
97	
98	The exact product identity
99	\[
100	\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
101	=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
102	\]
103	and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
104	most
105	\[
106	|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
107	\]
108	where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
109	\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
110	each of its two terms, yields
111	\[
112	\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
113	\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
114	\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
115	\tag{8}
116	\]
117	In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).
118	
119	## Counting the truncated congruences
120	
121	For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
122	\[
123	n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
124	\]
125	are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
126	both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
127	the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
128	\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
129	\[
130	a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
131	\]
132	Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
133	\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
134	\[
135	h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
136	\]
137	For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
138	number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
139	\[
140	\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
141	-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
142	=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
143	\tag{9}
144	\]
145	This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).
146	
147	Define
148	\[
149	A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
150	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
151	\]
152	Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
153	\[
154	\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
155	\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
156	\tag{10}
157	\]
158	Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
159	at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
160	most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.
161	
162	## The infinite main term and its uniform tail
163	
164	Consider
165	\[
166	A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
167	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
168	\]
169	This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
170	with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
171	absolute sum by
172	\[
173	\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
174	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
175	   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
176	   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
177	\le8.
178	\tag{11}
179	\]
180	
181	We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
182	\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
183	\[
184	\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
185	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
186	  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
187	  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
188	\tag{12}
189	\]
190	For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
191	\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
192	and their total is at most
193	\[
194	\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
195	\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
196	\]
197	For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
198	\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
199	\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
200	\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
201	bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
202	\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
203	bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
204	\[
205	|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
206	=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
207	\tag{13}
208	\]
209	All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
210	\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).
211	
212	Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
213	one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
214	finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
215	exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
216	For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
217	follows:
218	
219	| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
220	| --- | --- | --- |
221	| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
222	| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
223	| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
224	| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |
225	
226	It follows that
227	\[
228	\begin{aligned}
229	A(m)
230	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
231	                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
232	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
233	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
234	  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
235	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
236	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
237	=\mathfrak S(m).
238	\end{aligned}
239	\tag{14}
240	\]
241	The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
242	because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.
243	
244	## Combining the bounds
245	
246	Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
247	\[
248	\begin{aligned}
249	L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
250	&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
251	&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
252	&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
253	\end{aligned}
254	\tag{15}
255	\]
256	For \(x\ge1\),
257	\[
258	\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
259	\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
260	=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
261	\]
262	Thus (15) is at most
263	\[
264	32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
265	\tag{16}
266	\]
267	Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
268	\[
269	\begin{aligned}
270	\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
271	&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
272	&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
273	\end{aligned}
274	\]
275	This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
276	\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
277	\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
278	\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
279	uniformity. \(\square\)

# Proof of P3

We prove the stronger bound
\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
\tag{1}
\]
with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.

## An explicit divisor bound

Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
\(n\). Define the absolute constant
\[
D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
\]
where the product is over primes. We will use
\[
\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
\tag{2}
\]
Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
\[
(a+1)p^{-a/10}
\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
\]
Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
all at least one.

We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
integers \(H\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
\tag{3}
\]
The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).

## Truncating the square-divisor identities

Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
\[
L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
\]
In particular,
\[
\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
\tag{4}
\]
For positive integers \(k\), define
\[
T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
\]
All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
\[
\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
\tag{5}
\]
follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
Also
\[
|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
\tag{6}
\]

For either of the two sets
\[
I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
\]
there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
\[
\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
\le\frac{x}{H}.
\tag{7}
\]
This estimate also holds when either set is empty.

The exact product identity
\[
\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
most
\[
|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
\]
where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
each of its two terms, yields
\[
\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).

## Counting the truncated congruences

For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
\[
n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
\[
a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
\]
Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
\[
h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
\]
For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
\tag{9}
\]
This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).

Define
\[
A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
\[
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.

## The infinite main term and its uniform tail

Consider
\[
A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
absolute sum by
\[
\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
\le8.
\tag{11}
\]

We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
\[
\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
\tag{12}
\]
For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
and their total is at most
\[
\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
\]
For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
\[
|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
\tag{13}
\]
All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).

Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
follows:

| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |

It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(m)
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
=\mathfrak S(m).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.

## Combining the bounds

Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
For \(x\ge1\),
\[
\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
\]
Thus (15) is at most
\[
32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\tag{16}
\]
Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
uniformity. \(\square\)

1	\chapter{Averaging over polynomial moduli}\label{ch:averaging}
2	
3	After \cref{ch:variance,ch:correlations} the variance is expressed through two sums over $k$: the density term $T_f(z,y)$ and the main part of the off-diagonal term,
4	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mf}
5	M_f(x;z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}\bigl(x-hf(k)\bigr)\Sing\bigl(hf(k)\bigr).
6	\end{equation}
7	Both involve arithmetic functions of $f(k)$. Expanding them over $r$ with the coefficients $\lambda(r)$ of \cref{ch:densities} makes the dependence on $k$ periodic modulo $r$. Partial summation then replaces the sum over $k$ by an integral in the variable $t=f(k)$, with $f'(k)$ acting as the Jacobian. This is the role of the weight $f'(k)$. (Archived source: proposition P4, a crux of the plan.)
8	
9	\section{The averaged singular series}
10	
11	For $h\ge1$ and a prime $p$ put
12	\[
13	\delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:\ p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
14	\]
15	If $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$, then $p^2\mid hf(a)$ is equivalent to $p^j\mid f(a)$. Counting lifts from residues modulo $p^j$ to residues modulo $p^2$ gives
16	\begin{equation}\label{eq:deltap}
17	\delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^{j})}{p^{j}}\in[0,1],\qquad\text{so}\qquad
18	1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
19	\end{equation}
20	where $w_p(h)$ is the local factor in \eqref{eq:W-intro}. Comparing with the second form of \eqref{eq:sing}, $W_f(h)=\prod_pw_p(h)$ is what one obtains by replacing the indicator $\one_{p^2\mid hf(k)}$ in $\Sing(hf(k))$ by its average $\delta_p(h)$ over $k$. \Cref{lem:W-ident} below makes this precise.
21	
22	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-basic}
23	For every $h\ge1$ and prime $p$, $1-2p^{-2}\le w_p(h)\le1-p^{-2}$. Hence the product $W_f(h)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $h$, and $0<W_f(h)\le1$. The series
24	\[
25	\widetilde R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
26	\]
27	converges absolutely and $0\le\widetilde R_f\le c$.
28	\end{lemma}
29	
30	\begin{proof}
31	The bounds for $w_p$ follow from $\delta_p(h)\in[0,1]$, so $|w_p(h)-1|\le2p^{-2}$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. The factors are positive, so $W_f(h)>0$, and they are at most one. Finally $0\le\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
32	\end{proof}
33	
34	For $r,h\ge1$ define
35	\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta}
36	\beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r\frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)},
37	\end{equation}
38	the mean value of the $r$-periodic sequence
39	\[
40	k\longmapsto\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
41	\]
42	Note $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ by \cref{lem:ramanujan}(b).
43	
44	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-ident}
45	For every $h\ge1$, $\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=W_f(h)$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly in $h$.
46	\end{lemma}
47	
48	\begin{proof}
49	Absolute and uniform convergence follow from $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$. If $(r,s)=1$, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies $a\bmod rs$ with pairs $(a\bmod r,\ a\bmod s)$. Moreover $c_{rs}=c_rc_s$, $c_r(hf(a))$ depends only on $a\bmod r$, and $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$. Hence $\beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)$. Thus $\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)$ is $c^2$ times a multiplicative function supported on cube-free $r$, and \cref{lem:euler} gives
50	\[
51	\sum_r\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=c^2\prod_p\Bigl(1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)
52	\]
53	by \eqref{eq:lambda-p}. The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ may equally be taken over $a\bmod p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. Therefore, by \eqref{eq:cp-sum},
54	\[
55	(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)=\frac1{p^2}\sum_{a\bmod p^2}\bigl(c_p+c_{p^2}\bigr)(hf(a))=p^2\delta_p(h)-1.
56	\]
57	Distributing $c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2$ over the primes, the local factor becomes
58	\[
59	\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2+p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{p^4}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
60	\]
61	by \eqref{eq:deltap}. No restriction on $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
62	\end{proof}
63	
64	\section{A partial summation lemma}
65	
66	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:periodic}
67	Let $b$ be a periodic sequence with integer period $r\ge1$, $|b(k)|\le1$, and mean $m_b=r^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^rb(a)$. Let $1\le u\le v$ be real and let $F$ be continuously differentiable on $[u,v]$. Then
68	\[
69	\Bigl|\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t\Bigr|\le4r\Bigl(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\dd t\Bigr).
70	\]
71	\end{lemma}
72	
73	\begin{proof}
74	Let $P(t)=\sum_{k\le t}b(k)-m_bt$. Writing $t=qr+s$ with $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\le s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel, the remaining at most $r$ terms have modulus at most $1$, and $|m_bs|\le r$; so $|P(t)|\le2r$. Hence $D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\le t}b(k)-m_b(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)$ satisfies $|D_u(t)|\le4r$ and $D_u(u)=0$. Riemann--Stieltjes integration by parts gives the identity
75	\[
76	\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t=\int_u^vF(t)\dd D_u(t)=F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\dd t,
77	\]
78	from which the bound follows.
79	\end{proof}
80	
81	With $F=w=f'/f$ on $[z,y]$, \cref{lem:poly}(b) gives $|w(y)|\le U/y\le U/z$ and $\int_z^y|w'|\le V/z$. Since $\int_z^yw=\log(Y/Z)$, we obtain for every $r$-periodic $b$ as in \cref{lem:periodic} and $1\le z\le y$:
82	\begin{equation}\label{eq:periodic-w}
83	\Bigl|\sum_{z<k\le y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}-m_b\log\frac YZ\Bigr|\le\frac{4D_wr}z,\qquad D_w=U+V.
84	\end{equation}
85	
86	\section{The averaging proposition}
87	
88	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:averaging}
89	There is $C(f)>0$ such that the following holds uniformly for real $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ with $Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$, and real $2\le R\le x$. With
90	\[
91	\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)
92	\]
93	and
94	\begin{equation}\label{eq:If}
95	I_f(x;Z,Y)=\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\dd t,
96	\end{equation}
97	we have
98	\begin{align}
99	\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,\mathcal A,\label{eq:avg1}\\
100	\bigl|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,x^2\mathcal A.\label{eq:avg2}
101	\end{align}
102	No condition on the discriminant, content or factorisation of $f$ is imposed.
103	\end{proposition}
104	
105	Throughout the proof, $\mathcal T(R)$ and $\mathcal N(R)$ are as in \cref{prop:second-moment}(d), so that $\mathcal T(R)\le C_0R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2$ and $\mathcal N(R)\le C_0R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2$. If $z=y$ both assertions are trivial, so we assume $z<y$.
106	
107	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg1}]
108	By \cref{prop:second-moment}(a) applied to $q=f(k)$,
109	\[
110	T_f(z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
111	\]
112	The part with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most $\mathcal T(R)\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)/f(k)\le2U\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$ by \eqref{eq:sum-w}. For each $r\le R$, the sequence $b(k)=\one_{r\mid f(k)}$ has period $r$ and mean $\rho(r)/r$, so \eqref{eq:periodic-w} gives
113	\[
114	\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\one_{r\mid f(k)}=\frac{\rho(r)}r\log\frac YZ+e_r,\qquad|e_r|\le\frac{4D_wr}z.
115	\]
116	Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ produces an error at most $4D_w\mathcal N(R)/z$. Completing $\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$ to $\widetilde R_f$ costs at most $\mathcal T(R)\log(Y/Z)\le\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$, because $\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. Since $Z\le\kappa_2z^d$, we have $z^{-1}\le\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}$, and therefore
117	\[
118	\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|\le C_0\Bigl(4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).\qedhere
119	\]
120	\end{proof}
121	
122	For the second assertion we first need a bound for the weight functions. Let $H_0=\lfloor x/Z\rfloor$. For $1\le h\le H_0$ define
123	\[
124	v_h=\min\{y,\,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad F_h(t)=f'(t)\bigl(x-hf(t)\bigr)\quad(z\le t\le v_h),
125	\]
126	which is legitimate because $x/h\ge Z=f(z)$ (\cref{lem:poly}(a)). Then $z\le v_h\le(x/(\kappa_1h))^{1/d}$ and $0\le x-hf(t)\le x$ on $[z,v_h]$. Put
127	\[
128	K_2=\begin{cases}\kappa_2+\kappa_2^2/\kappa_1,&d=1,\\ \kappa_2+\kappa_2/(d-1)+\kappa_2^2/((2d-1)\kappa_1),&d\ge2.\end{cases}
129	\]
130	
131	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:weight-var}
132	For $1\le h\le H_0$, $\displaystyle|F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\dd t\le K_2\,x\,v_h^{d-1}$.
133	\end{lemma}
134	
135	\begin{proof}
136	We have $|F_h(v_h)|\le\kappa_2xv_h^{d-1}$ and $|F_h'|\le|f''|(x-hf)+hf'^2$. For $d\ge2$,
137	\[
138	\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le\kappa_2x\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\dd t+h\kappa_2^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\dd t\le\frac{\kappa_2}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}+\frac{h\kappa_2^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1},
139	\]
140	and $hv_h^d\le x/\kappa_1$ bounds the last term by $\kappa_2^2xv_h^{d-1}/((2d-1)\kappa_1)$. For $d=1$, $f''=0$ and $\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le h\kappa_2^2v_h\le\kappa_2^2x/\kappa_1$.
141	\end{proof}
142	
143	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg2}]
144	\emph{Truncation in $r$.} Put
145	\[
146	\Sing_R(n)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad W_R(h)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
147	\]
148	By \cref{prop:ramanujan-sing,lem:W-ident} and the bounds $|c_r(n)|\le\varphi(r)$ and $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$,
149	\[
150	|\Sing(n)-\Sing_R(n)|\le\mathcal T(R),\qquad|W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\le\mathcal T(R)
151	\]
152	uniformly in $n,h$. Let $M_R$ and $I_R$ be $M_f$ and $I_f$ with $\Sing$ and $W_f$ replaced by $\Sing_R$ and $W_R$. For fixed $k$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ values of $h$, each with $0\le x-hf(k)\le x$, so by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
153	\[
154	|M_f-M_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le2U\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x).
155	\]
156	Similarly, for each $t\in[Z,Y]$ there are at most $x/t$ values of $h$, so $|I_f-I_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\int_Z^Y\dd t/t\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x)$.
157	
158	\emph{The finite approximations.} All remaining sums are finite and may be rearranged. For integers $k\in(z,y]$, the condition $h\le x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\le v_h$, and $k>z$ forces $h<x/Z$. Hence
159	\[
160	M_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\sum_{z<k\le v_h}F_h(k)\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
161	\]
162	The sequence $k\mapsto c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)$ has period $r$, because $f$ has integer coefficients, and its mean is $\beta_r(h)$. The substitution $t=f(u)$ gives
163	\[
164	\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u=\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\dd t,
165	\]
166	and therefore $I_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u$. By \cref{lem:periodic,lem:weight-var}, the inner difference for fixed $r$ and $h$ is at most $4rK_2xv_h^{d-1}\le4rK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}$. If $v_h=z$ the difference is zero. By \cref{lem:sums}(e), $\sum_{h\le H_0}h^{-1+1/d}\le d(x/Z)^{1/d}$, so for fixed $r$ the total difference is at most $K_3rx^2Z^{-1/d}$ with $K_3=4dK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}$. No logarithm arises here. Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ gives
167	\[
168	|M_R-I_R|\le K_3x^2Z^{-1/d}\mathcal N(R).
169	\]
170	
171	Combining the three estimates proves
172	\[
173	|M_f-I_f|\le C_0x^2\Bigl(K_3Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).
174	\]
175	Together with the first part, \cref{prop:averaging} holds with $C(f)=C_0\max\{4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d},K_3,2U+1\}$.
176	\end{proof}
177	
178	\begin{remark}
179	The error $x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}$ comes from the $k$-sampling of a weight of total variation about $xv_h^{d-1}$, summed over $h$ with the $h$-dependent endpoint $v_h$. The archived plan points out that using the endpoint $y$ for every $h$, instead of $v_h$, would lose the claimed range. The error is small only when $Z^{1/d}$, which is comparable to $z$, is large compared with $R$. Balancing this error against the tail $R^{-1/2}$ leads to the choice $R=Z^{1/d}$ in \cref{ch:assembly}.
180	\end{remark}
181
