\chapter{Averaging over polynomial moduli}\label{ch:averaging}

After \cref{ch:variance,ch:correlations} the variance is expressed through two sums over $k$: the density term $T_f(z,y)$ and the main part of the off-diagonal term,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mf}
M_f(x;z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}\bigl(x-hf(k)\bigr)\Sing\bigl(hf(k)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Both involve arithmetic functions of $f(k)$. Expanding them over $r$ with the coefficients $\lambda(r)$ of \cref{ch:densities} makes the dependence on $k$ periodic modulo $r$. Partial summation then replaces the sum over $k$ by an integral in the variable $t=f(k)$, with $f'(k)$ acting as the Jacobian. This is the role of the weight $f'(k)$. (Archived source: proposition P4, a crux of the plan.)

\section{The averaged singular series}

For $h\ge1$ and a prime $p$ put
\[
\delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:\ p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
\]
If $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$, then $p^2\mid hf(a)$ is equivalent to $p^j\mid f(a)$. Counting lifts from residues modulo $p^j$ to residues modulo $p^2$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deltap}
\delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^{j})}{p^{j}}\in[0,1],\qquad\text{so}\qquad
1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
\end{equation}
where $w_p(h)$ is the local factor in \eqref{eq:W-intro}. Comparing with the second form of \eqref{eq:sing}, $W_f(h)=\prod_pw_p(h)$ is what one obtains by replacing the indicator $\one_{p^2\mid hf(k)}$ in $\Sing(hf(k))$ by its average $\delta_p(h)$ over $k$. \Cref{lem:W-ident} below makes this precise.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-basic}
For every $h\ge1$ and prime $p$, $1-2p^{-2}\le w_p(h)\le1-p^{-2}$. Hence the product $W_f(h)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $h$, and $0<W_f(h)\le1$. The series
\[
\widetilde R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
\]
converges absolutely and $0\le\widetilde R_f\le c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The bounds for $w_p$ follow from $\delta_p(h)\in[0,1]$, so $|w_p(h)-1|\le2p^{-2}$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. The factors are positive, so $W_f(h)>0$, and they are at most one. Finally $0\le\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
\end{proof}

For $r,h\ge1$ define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta}
\beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r\frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)},
\end{equation}
the mean value of the $r$-periodic sequence
\[
k\longmapsto\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
\]
Note $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ by \cref{lem:ramanujan}(b).

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-ident}
For every $h\ge1$, $\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=W_f(h)$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly in $h$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Absolute and uniform convergence follow from $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$. If $(r,s)=1$, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies $a\bmod rs$ with pairs $(a\bmod r,\ a\bmod s)$. Moreover $c_{rs}=c_rc_s$, $c_r(hf(a))$ depends only on $a\bmod r$, and $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$. Hence $\beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)$. Thus $\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)$ is $c^2$ times a multiplicative function supported on cube-free $r$, and \cref{lem:euler} gives
\[
\sum_r\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=c^2\prod_p\Bigl(1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)
\]
by \eqref{eq:lambda-p}. The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ may equally be taken over $a\bmod p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. Therefore, by \eqref{eq:cp-sum},
\[
(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)=\frac1{p^2}\sum_{a\bmod p^2}\bigl(c_p+c_{p^2}\bigr)(hf(a))=p^2\delta_p(h)-1.
\]
Distributing $c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2$ over the primes, the local factor becomes
\[
\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2+p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{p^4}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
\]
by \eqref{eq:deltap}. No restriction on $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
\end{proof}

\section{A partial summation lemma}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:periodic}
Let $b$ be a periodic sequence with integer period $r\ge1$, $|b(k)|\le1$, and mean $m_b=r^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^rb(a)$. Let $1\le u\le v$ be real and let $F$ be continuously differentiable on $[u,v]$. Then
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t\Bigr|\le4r\Bigl(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\dd t\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $P(t)=\sum_{k\le t}b(k)-m_bt$. Writing $t=qr+s$ with $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\le s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel, the remaining at most $r$ terms have modulus at most $1$, and $|m_bs|\le r$; so $|P(t)|\le2r$. Hence $D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\le t}b(k)-m_b(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)$ satisfies $|D_u(t)|\le4r$ and $D_u(u)=0$. Riemann--Stieltjes integration by parts gives the identity
\[
\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t=\int_u^vF(t)\dd D_u(t)=F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\dd t,
\]
from which the bound follows.
\end{proof}

With $F=w=f'/f$ on $[z,y]$, \cref{lem:poly}(b) gives $|w(y)|\le U/y\le U/z$ and $\int_z^y|w'|\le V/z$. Since $\int_z^yw=\log(Y/Z)$, we obtain for every $r$-periodic $b$ as in \cref{lem:periodic} and $1\le z\le y$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:periodic-w}
\Bigl|\sum_{z<k\le y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}-m_b\log\frac YZ\Bigr|\le\frac{4D_wr}z,\qquad D_w=U+V.
\end{equation}

\section{The averaging proposition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:averaging}
There is $C(f)>0$ such that the following holds uniformly for real $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ with $Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$, and real $2\le R\le x$. With
\[
\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:If}
I_f(x;Z,Y)=\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\dd t,
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{align}
\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,\mathcal A,\label{eq:avg1}\\
\bigl|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,x^2\mathcal A.\label{eq:avg2}
\end{align}
No condition on the discriminant, content or factorisation of $f$ is imposed.
\end{proposition}

Throughout the proof, $\mathcal T(R)$ and $\mathcal N(R)$ are as in \cref{prop:second-moment}(d), so that $\mathcal T(R)\le C_0R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2$ and $\mathcal N(R)\le C_0R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2$. If $z=y$ both assertions are trivial, so we assume $z<y$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg1}]
By \cref{prop:second-moment}(a) applied to $q=f(k)$,
\[
T_f(z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
\]
The part with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most $\mathcal T(R)\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)/f(k)\le2U\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$ by \eqref{eq:sum-w}. For each $r\le R$, the sequence $b(k)=\one_{r\mid f(k)}$ has period $r$ and mean $\rho(r)/r$, so \eqref{eq:periodic-w} gives
\[
\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\one_{r\mid f(k)}=\frac{\rho(r)}r\log\frac YZ+e_r,\qquad|e_r|\le\frac{4D_wr}z.
\]
Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ produces an error at most $4D_w\mathcal N(R)/z$. Completing $\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$ to $\widetilde R_f$ costs at most $\mathcal T(R)\log(Y/Z)\le\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$, because $\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. Since $Z\le\kappa_2z^d$, we have $z^{-1}\le\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}$, and therefore
\[
\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|\le C_0\Bigl(4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

For the second assertion we first need a bound for the weight functions. Let $H_0=\lfloor x/Z\rfloor$. For $1\le h\le H_0$ define
\[
v_h=\min\{y,\,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad F_h(t)=f'(t)\bigl(x-hf(t)\bigr)\quad(z\le t\le v_h),
\]
which is legitimate because $x/h\ge Z=f(z)$ (\cref{lem:poly}(a)). Then $z\le v_h\le(x/(\kappa_1h))^{1/d}$ and $0\le x-hf(t)\le x$ on $[z,v_h]$. Put
\[
K_2=\begin{cases}\kappa_2+\kappa_2^2/\kappa_1,&d=1,\\ \kappa_2+\kappa_2/(d-1)+\kappa_2^2/((2d-1)\kappa_1),&d\ge2.\end{cases}
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:weight-var}
For $1\le h\le H_0$, $\displaystyle|F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\dd t\le K_2\,x\,v_h^{d-1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We have $|F_h(v_h)|\le\kappa_2xv_h^{d-1}$ and $|F_h'|\le|f''|(x-hf)+hf'^2$. For $d\ge2$,
\[
\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le\kappa_2x\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\dd t+h\kappa_2^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\dd t\le\frac{\kappa_2}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}+\frac{h\kappa_2^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1},
\]
and $hv_h^d\le x/\kappa_1$ bounds the last term by $\kappa_2^2xv_h^{d-1}/((2d-1)\kappa_1)$. For $d=1$, $f''=0$ and $\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le h\kappa_2^2v_h\le\kappa_2^2x/\kappa_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg2}]
\emph{Truncation in $r$.} Put
\[
\Sing_R(n)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad W_R(h)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
\]
By \cref{prop:ramanujan-sing,lem:W-ident} and the bounds $|c_r(n)|\le\varphi(r)$ and $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$,
\[
|\Sing(n)-\Sing_R(n)|\le\mathcal T(R),\qquad|W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\le\mathcal T(R)
\]
uniformly in $n,h$. Let $M_R$ and $I_R$ be $M_f$ and $I_f$ with $\Sing$ and $W_f$ replaced by $\Sing_R$ and $W_R$. For fixed $k$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ values of $h$, each with $0\le x-hf(k)\le x$, so by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
\[
|M_f-M_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le2U\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x).
\]
Similarly, for each $t\in[Z,Y]$ there are at most $x/t$ values of $h$, so $|I_f-I_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\int_Z^Y\dd t/t\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x)$.

\emph{The finite approximations.} All remaining sums are finite and may be rearranged. For integers $k\in(z,y]$, the condition $h\le x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\le v_h$, and $k>z$ forces $h<x/Z$. Hence
\[
M_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\sum_{z<k\le v_h}F_h(k)\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
\]
The sequence $k\mapsto c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)$ has period $r$, because $f$ has integer coefficients, and its mean is $\beta_r(h)$. The substitution $t=f(u)$ gives
\[
\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u=\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\dd t,
\]
and therefore $I_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u$. By \cref{lem:periodic,lem:weight-var}, the inner difference for fixed $r$ and $h$ is at most $4rK_2xv_h^{d-1}\le4rK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}$. If $v_h=z$ the difference is zero. By \cref{lem:sums}(e), $\sum_{h\le H_0}h^{-1+1/d}\le d(x/Z)^{1/d}$, so for fixed $r$ the total difference is at most $K_3rx^2Z^{-1/d}$ with $K_3=4dK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}$. No logarithm arises here. Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ gives
\[
|M_R-I_R|\le K_3x^2Z^{-1/d}\mathcal N(R).
\]

Combining the three estimates proves
\[
|M_f-I_f|\le C_0x^2\Bigl(K_3Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).
\]
Together with the first part, \cref{prop:averaging} holds with $C(f)=C_0\max\{4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d},K_3,2U+1\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The error $x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}$ comes from the $k$-sampling of a weight of total variation about $xv_h^{d-1}$, summed over $h$ with the $h$-dependent endpoint $v_h$. The archived plan points out that using the endpoint $y$ for every $h$, instead of $v_h$, would lose the claimed range. The error is small only when $Z^{1/d}$, which is comparable to $z$, is large compared with $R$. Balancing this error against the tail $R^{-1/2}$ leads to the choice $R=Z^{1/d}$ in \cref{ch:assembly}.
\end{remark}

1	# Proof of P4
2	
3	We use P1 exactly as supplied. No external paper is used. All logarithms are natural. Constants introduced below depend only on $f$, except for the absolute constant supplied by P1.
4	
5	## Polynomial bounds and a periodic averaging lemma
6	
7	The leading coefficient of $f$ is positive: otherwise $f(t)\geq 2$ for all $t\geq 1$ would fail. Since $f(t)>0$ on this interval, continuity and the positive limit of $f(t)/t^d$ give constants $a>0$ and $B\geq 1$ such that, for every $t\geq 1$,
8	\[
9	 a t^d\leq f(t)\leq B t^d,
10	 \qquad |f'(t)|\leq B t^{d-1}.
11	 \tag{1}
12	\]
13	When $d\geq 2$, enlarge $B$ so that
14	\[
15	 |f''(t)|\leq B t^{d-2}\quad(t\geq 1).
16	 \tag{2}
17	\]
18	When $d=1$, $f''=0$. Define
19	\[
20	 U=\frac{B}{a},\qquad
21	 V=\frac{B}{a}+\frac{B^2}{a^2},\qquad D=U+V.
22	 \tag{3}
23	\]
24	For $w(t)=f'(t)/f(t)$, equations (1)--(2), including $f''=0$ when $d=1$, imply
25	\[
26	 0<w(t)\leq\frac{U}{t},\qquad
27	 |w'(t)|
28	 \leq\frac{|f''(t)|}{f(t)}+\frac{|f'(t)|^2}{f(t)^2}
29	 \leq\frac{V}{t^2}.
30	 \tag{4}
31	\]
32	Also $f'(t)\geq 1$ and $f(1)\geq 2$ give $f(t)\geq t+1$. Thus $y<x$, and
33	\[
34	 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
35	 \leq U\sum_{1\leq k\leq y}\frac1k
36	 \leq U(1+\log y)
37	 \leq 2U\log(2x).
38	 \tag{5}
39	\]
40	Here the sum has at most $\lfloor y\rfloor\leq\lfloor x\rfloor$ terms; the harmonic-sum bound follows by comparison with the integral of $1/t$ on $[1,y]$.
41	
42	We will use the following elementary lemma. If $b(k)$ is periodic of integer period $r\geq 1$, satisfies $|b(k)|\leq 1$, and has mean
43	\[
44	 m=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r b(a),
45	\]
46	then, for real $1\leq u\leq v$ and a continuously differentiable function $F$ on $[u,v]$,
47	\[
48	 \left|\sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^v F(t)\,dt\right|
49	 \leq 4r\left(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\,dt\right).
50	 \tag{6}
51	\]
52	To prove this, put
53	\[
54	 P(t)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}b(k)-mt.
55	\]
56	Writing $t=qr+s$, where $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\leq s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel. The remaining sum has at most $r$ terms of modulus at most $1$, and $|ms|\leq r$. Hence $|P(t)|\leq 2r$. Consequently
57	\[
58	 D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\leq t}b(k)-m(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)
59	 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad |D_u(t)|\leq 4r.
60	\]
61	Integration by parts gives the exact identity
62	\[
63	 \sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^vF(t)\,dt
64	 =F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\,dt,
65	\]
66	which proves (6), with the indicated convention at both endpoints.
67	
68	For later use, (4) and (6) yield
69	\[
70	 \left|\sum_{z<k\leq y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
71	       -m\log(Y/Z)\right|
72	 \leq \frac{4Dr}{z}.
73	 \tag{7}
74	\]
75	Indeed, $|w(y)|\leq U/z$, while
76	\(
77	\int_z^y |w'(t)|\,dt\leq V/z.
78	\)
79	These bounds also cover $z=y$; in that case the two conclusions of P4 are immediate. We may henceforth take $z<y$.
80	
81	## Spectral notation and the common density
82	
83	Let $c_r(n)$, $\gamma(r)$, and $\lambda(r)$ have the meanings in P1. Since
84	\(
85	\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)\gamma(r)^2
86	\)
87	and $c_r(n)$ is a sum of $\varphi(r)$ complex numbers of modulus $1$,
88	\[
89	 |c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
90	 \mathfrak S(n)=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)}.
91	 \tag{8}
92	\]
93	In particular, P1 gives absolute convergence, uniformly in $n\geq 1$, because $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
94	
95	For $h\geq 1$, define
96	\[
97	 \beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r
98	           \frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)}.
99	 \tag{9}
100	\]
101	Thus $|\beta_r(h)|\leq 1$, and
102	\[
103	 \mathcal W(h):=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)
104	 \tag{10}
105	\]
106	converges absolutely and uniformly in $h\geq 1$. We now prove that
107	\[
108	 \mathcal W(h)=W_f(h).
109	 \tag{11}
110	\]
111	
112	For completeness, the elementary Ramanujan-sum identities needed here follow directly from finite sums. Inserting
113	\(
114	\mathbf 1_{(a,r)=1}=\sum_{b\mid(a,r)}\mu(b)
115	\)
116	into the definition of $c_r(n)$, and summing the resulting geometric progression, gives
117	\[
118	 c_r(n)
119	 =\sum_{b\mid r}\mu(b)
120	       \sum_{a'=1}^{r/b}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i a'n}{r/b}\right)
121	 =\sum_{s\mid(r,n)}s\mu(r/s).
122	 \tag{12}
123	\]
124	Factoring this divisor sum over two coprime moduli shows that $c_{rs}(n)=c_r(n)c_s(n)$ when $(r,s)=1$. The Chinese remainder theorem, applied to the complete average in (9), therefore gives
125	\[
126	 \beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)\quad((r,s)=1).
127	 \tag{13}
128	\]
129	Here we also use $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$, which follows by counting invertible residue classes under the same bijection.
130	
131	The function $\lambda(r)/c^2$ is multiplicative, is supported on integers with no prime cube divisor, and has prime-power values
132	\[
133	 \frac{\lambda(p)}{c^2}=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
134	 \frac{\lambda(p^2)}{c^2}=\frac{p^2-p}{(p^2-1)^2}.
135	 \tag{14}
136	\]
137	The absolute convergence in (10) and (13)--(14) permit its Euler product. Equations (12) give, for each integer $n$,
138	\[
139	 c_p(n)=p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}-1,
140	 \qquad
141	 c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n},
142	\]
143	and hence
144	\[
145	 c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
146	 \tag{15}
147	\]
148	Put
149	\[
150	 \delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
151	\]
152	The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ can also be taken modulo $p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. It follows from (14)--(15) that the local factor, before including the local factor of $c^2$, is
153	\[
154	 1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}
155	 =1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}.
156	 \tag{16}
157	\]
158	
159	Write $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$. If $j=2$, the condition is $p^2\mid f(a)$, so there are $\rho(p^2)$ classes modulo $p^2$. If $j=1$, the condition is $p\mid f(a)$, and each of its $\rho(p)$ classes modulo $p$ has $p$ lifts modulo $p^2$. If $j=0$, every class is allowed. Using $\rho(1)=1$, the three cases give
160	\[
161	 \delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^j)}{p^j},\qquad 0\leq\delta_p(h)\leq 1.
162	 \tag{17}
163	\]
164	No restriction on the coefficients of $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
165	
166	Unique factorization and the absolutely convergent geometric series for each prime give
167	\(
168	c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2.
169	\)
170	Multiplying (16) by its local factor gives the exact identity
171	\[
172	 \begin{aligned}
173	 (1-p^{-2})^2
174	 \left(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
175	 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}\\
176	 &=(1-2p^{-2})
177	       \left(1+\frac{\rho(p^{j_p(h)})}
178	       {p^{j_p(h)}(p^2-2)}\right).
179	 \end{aligned}
180	 \tag{18}
181	\]
182	This proves (11). All product rearrangements are absolute: the deviation from $1$ of the first expression on the right of (18) is at most $2/p^2$, and the added term in the second factor is at most
183	\(
184	1/(p^2-2)\leq 2/p^2.
185	\)
186	The sum of these bounds over primes is finite. This proves the asserted absolute convergence of $W_f(h)$. For the product defining $\mathfrak S(n)$, its local factor is
187	$1-2/p^2+\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}/p^2$, whose deviation from $1$ is at most $2/p^2$; its product therefore converges absolutely as well. Finally,
188	\[
189	 0\leq\frac{\rho(r)}r\leq 1,
190	 \qquad
191	 \sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
192	 \leq\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)=c,
193	 \tag{19}
194	\]
195	which proves absolute convergence of $R_f$.
196	
197	For real $R\geq 2$, set
198	\[
199	 L_R=(\log(2R))^2,\qquad
200	 T_R=\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r),\qquad
201	 M_R=\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r).
202	\]
203	By P1 there is an absolute $C_0>0$ such that
204	\[
205	 T_R\leq C_0R^{-1/2}L_R,
206	 \qquad M_R\leq C_0R^{1/2}L_R.
207	 \tag{20}
208	\]
209	
210	## The first averaging assertion
211	
212	For each positive integer $r$, the sequence
213	\(
214	b(k)=\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
215	\)
216	has period $r$, modulus at most $1$, and mean $\rho(r)/r$. Thus (7) gives
217	\[
218	 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
219	 =\frac{\rho(r)}r\log(Y/Z)+e_r,
220	 \qquad |e_r|\leq\frac{4Dr}{z}.
221	 \tag{21}
222	\]
223	The first identity for the squared densities in P1 applies to $q=f(k)$, which is a positive integer. Therefore, writing the expression to be estimated as $S_1$,
224	\[
225	 \begin{aligned}
226	 S_1
227	 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}f'(k)\sum_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)^2\\
228	 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
229	                     \sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
230	 \end{aligned}
231	 \tag{22}
232	\]
233	The part in (22) with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most
234	\[
235	 T_R\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
236	 \leq 2U T_R\log(2x)
237	 \tag{23}
238	\]
239	by (5). This uses at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$; before summing, the bound for each such value is $T_R f'(k)/f(k)\leq U T_R/k$.
240	
241	For $r\leq R$, there are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices. Before summing, the error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ in (21) is at most $4Dr\lambda(r)/z$. After summing it is at most $4DM_R/z$. Equations (21)--(23) consequently give
242	\[
243	 \left|S_1-\log(Y/Z)\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r\right|
244	 \leq\frac{4DM_R}{z}+2U T_R\log(2x).
245	 \tag{24}
246	\]
247	For the infinite omitted part of the density coefficient, (19) gives the bound $\lambda(r)\log(Y/Z)$ at each index $r>R$, and summing gives
248	\[
249	 \log(Y/Z)\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
250	 \leq T_R\log(2x),
251	 \tag{25}
252	\]
253	since $2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x$. As $Z\leq Bz^d$, we have
254	\(
255	z^{-1}\leq B^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}.
256	\)
257	Combining (20), (24), and (25) proves the explicit bound
258	\[
259	 \boxed{
260	 |S_1-R_f\log(Y/Z)|
261	 \leq C_0\left(
262	 4DB^{1/d} Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
263	 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
264	 \right).}
265	 \tag{26}
266	\]
267	
268	## A weight bound for the second assertion
269	
270	Let
271	\[
272	 H=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{Z}\right\rfloor.
273	\]
274	Since $f'(t)\geq 1$, $f$ has a continuous increasing inverse on $[f(1),\infty)$. For $1\leq h\leq H$, define
275	\[
276	 v_h=\min\{y,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad
277	 F_h(t)=f'(t)(x-hf(t))\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
278	 \tag{27}
279	\]
280	These definitions are valid because $x/h\geq Z=f(z)$. They give
281	\[
282	 z\leq v_h\leq (x/(ah))^{1/d},\qquad
283	 0\leq x-hf(t)\leq x\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
284	 \tag{28}
285	\]
286	Define a constant $K$ by
287	\[
288	 K=
289	 \begin{cases}
290	 B+B^2/a,&d=1,\\[2mm]
291	 B+B/(d-1)+B^2/((2d-1)a),&d\geq 2.
292	 \end{cases}
293	 \tag{29}
294	\]
295	We claim
296	\[
297	 |F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
298	 \leq Kxv_h^{d-1}.
299	 \tag{30}
300	\]
301	For $d\geq 2$, (1)--(2) and (28) give
302	\[
303	 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bxv_h^{d-1},
304	\]
305	and
306	\[
307	 \begin{aligned}
308	 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
309	 &\leq\int_z^{v_h}
310	       \left(|f''(t)|(x-hf(t))+h|f'(t)|^2\right)\,dt\\
311	 &\leq Bx\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\,dt
312	       +hB^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\,dt\\
313	 &\leq\frac{B}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}
314	       +\frac{hB^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1}\\
315	 &\leq\left(\frac{B}{d-1}+\frac{B^2}{(2d-1)a}\right)
316	          xv_h^{d-1}.
317	 \end{aligned}
318	 \tag{31}
319	\]
320	The last inequality uses $hv_h^d\leq x/a$, from (28). For $d=1$, $f''=0$ gives
321	\[
322	 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bx,\qquad
323	 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
324	 \leq hB^2(v_h-z)\leq hB^2v_h\leq B^2x/a.
325	 \tag{32}
326	\]
327	Thus (30) holds for every $d\geq 1$.
328	
329	Apply (6) to
330	\(
331	b(k)=c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)
332	\)
333	with mean $\beta_r(h)$. This sequence has period $r$ because $f$ has integer coefficients. Equations (28)--(30) give
334	\[
335	 \begin{aligned}
336	 &\left|\sum_{z<k\leq v_h}
337	     f'(k)(x-hf(k))\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}
338	   -\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du\right|\\
339	 &\hspace{15mm}\leq
340	 4Kr x v_h^{d-1}
341	 \leq 4K a^{-(d-1)/d} r x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}.
342	 \end{aligned}
343	 \tag{33}
344	\]
345	If $v_h=z$, the left side is zero and this bound still applies.
346	
347	The $h$-sum has exactly $H\leq x/Z$ indices. The bound in (33) is the bound before summing. To sum it, the function $t^{-1+1/d}$ is nonincreasing and integrable on $(0,H]$, and therefore
348	\[
349	 \sum_{h=1}^{H}h^{-1+1/d}
350	 \leq\int_0^H t^{-1+1/d}\,dt
351	 =dH^{1/d}\leq d(x/Z)^{1/d}.
352	 \tag{34}
353	\]
354	This includes $d=1$, when the first inequality is equality. Combining (33)--(34), the error after summing over $h$ is at most
355	\[
356	 K_2 r x^2 Z^{-1/d},\qquad
357	 K_2=4Kd\,a^{-(d-1)/d}.
358	 \tag{35}
359	\]
360	In particular no logarithm is introduced by this sum.
361	
362	## The second averaging assertion
363	
364	Define the finite approximations
365	\[
366	 \mathfrak S_R(n)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)
367	                         \frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad
368	 W_R(h)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
369	\]
370	Equations (8)--(11) give, uniformly for positive integers $n,h$,
371	\[
372	 |\mathfrak S(n)-\mathfrak S_R(n)|\leq T_R,
373	 \qquad |W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\leq T_R.
374	 \tag{36}
375	\]
376	
377	Let $S_2$ denote the discrete expression in the second assertion and $I_2$ its integral expression. Define $S_{2,R}$ and $I_{2,R}$ by replacing $\mathfrak S$ and $W_f$ with $\mathfrak S_R$ and $W_R$, respectively.
378	
379	For a fixed integer $k$ with $z<k\leq y$, there are
380	\(
381	H_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\leq x/f(k)
382	\)
383	indices $h$. Before summing over $h$, the error from (36) is at most $T_R f'(k)(x-hf(k))\leq T_R x f'(k)$. After summing over these $H_k$ indices, it is at most
384	\(
385	T_R x^2 f'(k)/f(k).
386	\)
387	Summing this last bound over at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$ and using (5) gives
388	\[
389	 |S_2-S_{2,R}|\leq 2U T_R x^2\log(2x).
390	 \tag{37}
391	\]
392	For each $t\in[Z,Y]$, the $h$-sum has $\lfloor x/t\rfloor\leq x/t$ indices. Before summing, the error in an integrand term is at most $T_R(x-ht)\leq T_R x$. After summing it is at most $T_R x^2/t$. Integration gives
393	\[
394	 |I_2-I_{2,R}|
395	 \leq T_R x^2\int_Z^Y\frac{dt}{t}
396	 =T_R x^2\log(Y/Z)
397	 \leq T_R x^2\log(2x).
398	 \tag{38}
399	\]
400	
401	It remains to compare the finite approximations. All relevant sums are finite, so their orders can be interchanged. The change of variables $t=f(u)$ gives, for each $h\leq H$,
402	\[
403	 \int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du
404	 =\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\,dt.
405	 \tag{39}
406	\]
407	Moreover, for integer $k$ in $(z,y]$, the condition $h\leq x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\leq v_h$. Thus (35) compares the entire $h$-sum at a fixed $r$ in $S_{2,R}$ with its counterpart in $I_{2,R}$. Before summing over $r$, its error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ is at most
408	\(
409	K_2r\lambda(r)x^2 Z^{-1/d}.
410	\)
411	There are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices $r\leq R$; after summing, (20) gives
412	\[
413	 |S_{2,R}-I_{2,R}|
414	 \leq K_2x^2Z^{-1/d}M_R
415	 \leq C_0K_2 x^2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R.
416	 \tag{40}
417	\]
418	Combining (20) and (37)--(40) proves
419	\[
420	 \boxed{
421	 |S_2-I_2|
422	 \leq C_0 x^2\left(
423	 K_2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
424	 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
425	 \right).}
426	 \tag{41}
427	\]
428	
429	Finally, set
430	\[
431	 C(f)=C_0\max\{4DB^{1/d},\ K_2,\ 2U+1\}.
432	\]
433	With $A$ as in the statement, (26) is the first asserted inequality with right side $C(f)A$, and (41) is the second with right side $C(f)x^2A$. All constants are independent of $x,z,y,R$. Every estimate above is valid on the full stated ranges, including $d=1$ and polynomials with arbitrary content, discriminant, or factorization.
434	
435	## Numerical sanity checks and source record
436	
437	A Python check using exact rational arithmetic verified (18) for $p=2,3,5,7,11$ and each of the test densities $0,p^{-2},p^{-1},1$. A separate floating-point check verified the bound (34) for $d=1,\ldots,8$ and $H=1,2,10,1000$. These checks were only sanity checks; (18) and (34) were proved algebraically and by integration above.
438	
439	The only assumed proposition is the supplied P1. No published source or other run's artifacts were consulted; no excluded source was encountered. There were no supplied objections or previous-proof artifacts for this attempt.
440

# Proof of P4

We use P1 exactly as supplied. No external paper is used. All logarithms are natural. Constants introduced below depend only on $f$, except for the absolute constant supplied by P1.

## Polynomial bounds and a periodic averaging lemma

The leading coefficient of $f$ is positive: otherwise $f(t)\geq 2$ for all $t\geq 1$ would fail. Since $f(t)>0$ on this interval, continuity and the positive limit of $f(t)/t^d$ give constants $a>0$ and $B\geq 1$ such that, for every $t\geq 1$,
\[
 a t^d\leq f(t)\leq B t^d,
 \qquad |f'(t)|\leq B t^{d-1}.
 \tag{1}
\]
When $d\geq 2$, enlarge $B$ so that
\[
 |f''(t)|\leq B t^{d-2}\quad(t\geq 1).
 \tag{2}
\]
When $d=1$, $f''=0$. Define
\[
 U=\frac{B}{a},\qquad
 V=\frac{B}{a}+\frac{B^2}{a^2},\qquad D=U+V.
 \tag{3}
\]
For $w(t)=f'(t)/f(t)$, equations (1)--(2), including $f''=0$ when $d=1$, imply
\[
 0<w(t)\leq\frac{U}{t},\qquad
 |w'(t)|
 \leq\frac{|f''(t)|}{f(t)}+\frac{|f'(t)|^2}{f(t)^2}
 \leq\frac{V}{t^2}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Also $f'(t)\geq 1$ and $f(1)\geq 2$ give $f(t)\geq t+1$. Thus $y<x$, and
\[
 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \leq U\sum_{1\leq k\leq y}\frac1k
 \leq U(1+\log y)
 \leq 2U\log(2x).
 \tag{5}
\]
Here the sum has at most $\lfloor y\rfloor\leq\lfloor x\rfloor$ terms; the harmonic-sum bound follows by comparison with the integral of $1/t$ on $[1,y]$.

We will use the following elementary lemma. If $b(k)$ is periodic of integer period $r\geq 1$, satisfies $|b(k)|\leq 1$, and has mean
\[
 m=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r b(a),
\]
then, for real $1\leq u\leq v$ and a continuously differentiable function $F$ on $[u,v]$,
\[
 \left|\sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^v F(t)\,dt\right|
 \leq 4r\left(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\,dt\right).
 \tag{6}
\]
To prove this, put
\[
 P(t)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}b(k)-mt.
\]
Writing $t=qr+s$, where $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\leq s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel. The remaining sum has at most $r$ terms of modulus at most $1$, and $|ms|\leq r$. Hence $|P(t)|\leq 2r$. Consequently
\[
 D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\leq t}b(k)-m(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)
 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad |D_u(t)|\leq 4r.
\]
Integration by parts gives the exact identity
\[
 \sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^vF(t)\,dt
 =F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\,dt,
\]
which proves (6), with the indicated convention at both endpoints.

For later use, (4) and (6) yield
\[
 \left|\sum_{z<k\leq y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
       -m\log(Y/Z)\right|
 \leq \frac{4Dr}{z}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, $|w(y)|\leq U/z$, while
\(
\int_z^y |w'(t)|\,dt\leq V/z.
\)
These bounds also cover $z=y$; in that case the two conclusions of P4 are immediate. We may henceforth take $z<y$.

## Spectral notation and the common density

Let $c_r(n)$, $\gamma(r)$, and $\lambda(r)$ have the meanings in P1. Since
\(
\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)\gamma(r)^2
\)
and $c_r(n)$ is a sum of $\varphi(r)$ complex numbers of modulus $1$,
\[
 |c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
 \mathfrak S(n)=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)}.
 \tag{8}
\]
In particular, P1 gives absolute convergence, uniformly in $n\geq 1$, because $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.

For $h\geq 1$, define
\[
 \beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r
           \frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Thus $|\beta_r(h)|\leq 1$, and
\[
 \mathcal W(h):=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)
 \tag{10}
\]
converges absolutely and uniformly in $h\geq 1$. We now prove that
\[
 \mathcal W(h)=W_f(h).
 \tag{11}
\]

For completeness, the elementary Ramanujan-sum identities needed here follow directly from finite sums. Inserting
\(
\mathbf 1_{(a,r)=1}=\sum_{b\mid(a,r)}\mu(b)
\)
into the definition of $c_r(n)$, and summing the resulting geometric progression, gives
\[
 c_r(n)
 =\sum_{b\mid r}\mu(b)
       \sum_{a'=1}^{r/b}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i a'n}{r/b}\right)
 =\sum_{s\mid(r,n)}s\mu(r/s).
 \tag{12}
\]
Factoring this divisor sum over two coprime moduli shows that $c_{rs}(n)=c_r(n)c_s(n)$ when $(r,s)=1$. The Chinese remainder theorem, applied to the complete average in (9), therefore gives
\[
 \beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)\quad((r,s)=1).
 \tag{13}
\]
Here we also use $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$, which follows by counting invertible residue classes under the same bijection.

The function $\lambda(r)/c^2$ is multiplicative, is supported on integers with no prime cube divisor, and has prime-power values
\[
 \frac{\lambda(p)}{c^2}=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
 \frac{\lambda(p^2)}{c^2}=\frac{p^2-p}{(p^2-1)^2}.
 \tag{14}
\]
The absolute convergence in (10) and (13)--(14) permit its Euler product. Equations (12) give, for each integer $n$,
\[
 c_p(n)=p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}-1,
 \qquad
 c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n},
\]
and hence
\[
 c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
 \tag{15}
\]
Put
\[
 \delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
\]
The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ can also be taken modulo $p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. It follows from (14)--(15) that the local factor, before including the local factor of $c^2$, is
\[
 1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}
 =1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}.
 \tag{16}
\]

Write $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$. If $j=2$, the condition is $p^2\mid f(a)$, so there are $\rho(p^2)$ classes modulo $p^2$. If $j=1$, the condition is $p\mid f(a)$, and each of its $\rho(p)$ classes modulo $p$ has $p$ lifts modulo $p^2$. If $j=0$, every class is allowed. Using $\rho(1)=1$, the three cases give
\[
 \delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^j)}{p^j},\qquad 0\leq\delta_p(h)\leq 1.
 \tag{17}
\]
No restriction on the coefficients of $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.

Unique factorization and the absolutely convergent geometric series for each prime give
\(
c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2.
\)
Multiplying (16) by its local factor gives the exact identity
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (1-p^{-2})^2
 \left(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}\\
 &=(1-2p^{-2})
       \left(1+\frac{\rho(p^{j_p(h)})}
       {p^{j_p(h)}(p^2-2)}\right).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{18}
\]
This proves (11). All product rearrangements are absolute: the deviation from $1$ of the first expression on the right of (18) is at most $2/p^2$, and the added term in the second factor is at most
\(
1/(p^2-2)\leq 2/p^2.
\)
The sum of these bounds over primes is finite. This proves the asserted absolute convergence of $W_f(h)$. For the product defining $\mathfrak S(n)$, its local factor is
$1-2/p^2+\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}/p^2$, whose deviation from $1$ is at most $2/p^2$; its product therefore converges absolutely as well. Finally,
\[
 0\leq\frac{\rho(r)}r\leq 1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
 \leq\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)=c,
 \tag{19}
\]
which proves absolute convergence of $R_f$.

For real $R\geq 2$, set
\[
 L_R=(\log(2R))^2,\qquad
 T_R=\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r),\qquad
 M_R=\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r).
\]
By P1 there is an absolute $C_0>0$ such that
\[
 T_R\leq C_0R^{-1/2}L_R,
 \qquad M_R\leq C_0R^{1/2}L_R.
 \tag{20}
\]

## The first averaging assertion

For each positive integer $r$, the sequence
\(
b(k)=\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
\)
has period $r$, modulus at most $1$, and mean $\rho(r)/r$. Thus (7) gives
\[
 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
 =\frac{\rho(r)}r\log(Y/Z)+e_r,
 \qquad |e_r|\leq\frac{4Dr}{z}.
 \tag{21}
\]
The first identity for the squared densities in P1 applies to $q=f(k)$, which is a positive integer. Therefore, writing the expression to be estimated as $S_1$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_1
 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}f'(k)\sum_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)^2\\
 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
                     \sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{22}
\]
The part in (22) with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most
\[
 T_R\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \leq 2U T_R\log(2x)
 \tag{23}
\]
by (5). This uses at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$; before summing, the bound for each such value is $T_R f'(k)/f(k)\leq U T_R/k$.

For $r\leq R$, there are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices. Before summing, the error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ in (21) is at most $4Dr\lambda(r)/z$. After summing it is at most $4DM_R/z$. Equations (21)--(23) consequently give
\[
 \left|S_1-\log(Y/Z)\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r\right|
 \leq\frac{4DM_R}{z}+2U T_R\log(2x).
 \tag{24}
\]
For the infinite omitted part of the density coefficient, (19) gives the bound $\lambda(r)\log(Y/Z)$ at each index $r>R$, and summing gives
\[
 \log(Y/Z)\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
 \leq T_R\log(2x),
 \tag{25}
\]
since $2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x$. As $Z\leq Bz^d$, we have
\(
z^{-1}\leq B^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}.
\)
Combining (20), (24), and (25) proves the explicit bound
\[
 \boxed{
 |S_1-R_f\log(Y/Z)|
 \leq C_0\left(
 4DB^{1/d} Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
 \right).}
 \tag{26}
\]

## A weight bound for the second assertion

Let
\[
 H=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{Z}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since $f'(t)\geq 1$, $f$ has a continuous increasing inverse on $[f(1),\infty)$. For $1\leq h\leq H$, define
\[
 v_h=\min\{y,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad
 F_h(t)=f'(t)(x-hf(t))\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
 \tag{27}
\]
These definitions are valid because $x/h\geq Z=f(z)$. They give
\[
 z\leq v_h\leq (x/(ah))^{1/d},\qquad
 0\leq x-hf(t)\leq x\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
 \tag{28}
\]
Define a constant $K$ by
\[
 K=
 \begin{cases}
 B+B^2/a,&d=1,\\[2mm]
 B+B/(d-1)+B^2/((2d-1)a),&d\geq 2.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{29}
\]
We claim
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 \leq Kxv_h^{d-1}.
 \tag{30}
\]
For $d\geq 2$, (1)--(2) and (28) give
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bxv_h^{d-1},
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 &\leq\int_z^{v_h}
       \left(|f''(t)|(x-hf(t))+h|f'(t)|^2\right)\,dt\\
 &\leq Bx\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\,dt
       +hB^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\,dt\\
 &\leq\frac{B}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}
       +\frac{hB^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1}\\
 &\leq\left(\frac{B}{d-1}+\frac{B^2}{(2d-1)a}\right)
          xv_h^{d-1}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{31}
\]
The last inequality uses $hv_h^d\leq x/a$, from (28). For $d=1$, $f''=0$ gives
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bx,\qquad
 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 \leq hB^2(v_h-z)\leq hB^2v_h\leq B^2x/a.
 \tag{32}
\]
Thus (30) holds for every $d\geq 1$.

Apply (6) to
\(
b(k)=c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)
\)
with mean $\beta_r(h)$. This sequence has period $r$ because $f$ has integer coefficients. Equations (28)--(30) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left|\sum_{z<k\leq v_h}
     f'(k)(x-hf(k))\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}
   -\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du\right|\\
 &\hspace{15mm}\leq
 4Kr x v_h^{d-1}
 \leq 4K a^{-(d-1)/d} r x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{33}
\]
If $v_h=z$, the left side is zero and this bound still applies.

The $h$-sum has exactly $H\leq x/Z$ indices. The bound in (33) is the bound before summing. To sum it, the function $t^{-1+1/d}$ is nonincreasing and integrable on $(0,H]$, and therefore
\[
 \sum_{h=1}^{H}h^{-1+1/d}
 \leq\int_0^H t^{-1+1/d}\,dt
 =dH^{1/d}\leq d(x/Z)^{1/d}.
 \tag{34}
\]
This includes $d=1$, when the first inequality is equality. Combining (33)--(34), the error after summing over $h$ is at most
\[
 K_2 r x^2 Z^{-1/d},\qquad
 K_2=4Kd\,a^{-(d-1)/d}.
 \tag{35}
\]
In particular no logarithm is introduced by this sum.

## The second averaging assertion

Define the finite approximations
\[
 \mathfrak S_R(n)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)
                         \frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad
 W_R(h)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
\]
Equations (8)--(11) give, uniformly for positive integers $n,h$,
\[
 |\mathfrak S(n)-\mathfrak S_R(n)|\leq T_R,
 \qquad |W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\leq T_R.
 \tag{36}
\]

Let $S_2$ denote the discrete expression in the second assertion and $I_2$ its integral expression. Define $S_{2,R}$ and $I_{2,R}$ by replacing $\mathfrak S$ and $W_f$ with $\mathfrak S_R$ and $W_R$, respectively.

For a fixed integer $k$ with $z<k\leq y$, there are
\(
H_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\leq x/f(k)
\)
indices $h$. Before summing over $h$, the error from (36) is at most $T_R f'(k)(x-hf(k))\leq T_R x f'(k)$. After summing over these $H_k$ indices, it is at most
\(
T_R x^2 f'(k)/f(k).
\)
Summing this last bound over at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$ and using (5) gives
\[
 |S_2-S_{2,R}|\leq 2U T_R x^2\log(2x).
 \tag{37}
\]
For each $t\in[Z,Y]$, the $h$-sum has $\lfloor x/t\rfloor\leq x/t$ indices. Before summing, the error in an integrand term is at most $T_R(x-ht)\leq T_R x$. After summing it is at most $T_R x^2/t$. Integration gives
\[
 |I_2-I_{2,R}|
 \leq T_R x^2\int_Z^Y\frac{dt}{t}
 =T_R x^2\log(Y/Z)
 \leq T_R x^2\log(2x).
 \tag{38}
\]

It remains to compare the finite approximations. All relevant sums are finite, so their orders can be interchanged. The change of variables $t=f(u)$ gives, for each $h\leq H$,
\[
 \int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du
 =\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\,dt.
 \tag{39}
\]
Moreover, for integer $k$ in $(z,y]$, the condition $h\leq x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\leq v_h$. Thus (35) compares the entire $h$-sum at a fixed $r$ in $S_{2,R}$ with its counterpart in $I_{2,R}$. Before summing over $r$, its error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ is at most
\(
K_2r\lambda(r)x^2 Z^{-1/d}.
\)
There are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices $r\leq R$; after summing, (20) gives
\[
 |S_{2,R}-I_{2,R}|
 \leq K_2x^2Z^{-1/d}M_R
 \leq C_0K_2 x^2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R.
 \tag{40}
\]
Combining (20) and (37)--(40) proves
\[
 \boxed{
 |S_2-I_2|
 \leq C_0 x^2\left(
 K_2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
 \right).}
 \tag{41}
\]

Finally, set
\[
 C(f)=C_0\max\{4DB^{1/d},\ K_2,\ 2U+1\}.
\]
With $A$ as in the statement, (26) is the first asserted inequality with right side $C(f)A$, and (41) is the second with right side $C(f)x^2A$. All constants are independent of $x,z,y,R$. Every estimate above is valid on the full stated ranges, including $d=1$ and polynomials with arbitrary content, discriminant, or factorization.

## Numerical sanity checks and source record

A Python check using exact rational arithmetic verified (18) for $p=2,3,5,7,11$ and each of the test densities $0,p^{-2},p^{-1},1$. A separate floating-point check verified the bound (34) for $d=1,\ldots,8$ and $H=1,2,10,1000$. These checks were only sanity checks; (18) and (34) were proved algebraically and by integration above.

The only assumed proposition is the supplied P1. No published source or other run's artifacts were consulted; no excluded source was encountered. There were no supplied objections or previous-proof artifacts for this attempt.

1	\chapter{The Dirichlet series of the averaged singular series}\label{ch:dirichlet}
2	
3	The averaged singular series $W_f(h)$ is a product of local factors that depend only on whether $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. Its Dirichlet series therefore factors as $\zeta(s)$ times an Euler product, and a second factorisation exhibits a pole of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\frac12$. This pole, which is invisible in the region of absolute convergence, produces the main term of \cref{thm:main}. (Archived source: proposition P5, a crux of the plan.)
4	
5	\section{Facts about the zeta function}
6	
7	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zeta}
8	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
9	\item For every integer $N\ge1$ and $\re w>0$, $w\ne1$,
10	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-N}
11	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}-w\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-w-1}\dd u.
12	\end{equation}
13	In $\re w>0$ the only pole of $\zeta$ is a simple pole at $w=1$ with residue $1$, and $\lim_{w\to1}\bigl(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\bigr)=\gamma_E$, Euler's constant.
14	\item Let $\mathcal B_2(u)=\{u\}^2-\{u\}+\frac16$. The formula
15	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-B2}
16	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}-\frac{w(w+1)}2\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u
17	\end{equation}
18	continues $\zeta$ meromorphically to $\re w>-1$, with the single pole at $w=1$. In particular $\zeta(0)=-\frac12$ and $-\frac14\le\zeta(-\frac12)\le-\frac16$.
19	\end{enumerate}
20	\end{lemma}
21	
22	\begin{proof}
23	(a) For $\re w>1$ write $\sum_{n>N}n^{-w}=\int_N^\infty u^{-w}\dd\lfloor u\rfloor$, replace $\lfloor u\rfloor=u-\{u\}$, and integrate the second part by parts; the boundary term at $N$ vanishes because $\{N\}=0$. This gives \eqref{eq:zeta-N}. The integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $\re w>0$ because $0\le\{u\}<1$, which gives the continuation and the description of the pole. Subtracting $1/(w-1)$ and letting $w\to1$ gives $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N-\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-2}\dd u$. The integral lies in $[0,1/N]$, and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\gamma_E$ by its definition as $\lim(\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N)$.
24	
25	(b) With $N=1$, \eqref{eq:zeta-N} becomes $\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12-w\int_1^\infty(\{u\}-\frac12)u^{-w-1}\dd u$. The function $\mathcal B_2$ is continuous, satisfies $|\mathcal B_2|\le\frac16$, and has derivative $2(\{u\}-\frac12)$ between integers. Integration by parts over $[1,T]$ for integers $T\ge2$ gives
26	\[
27	\int_1^T\Bigl(\{u\}-\frac12\Bigr)u^{-w-1}\dd u=\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}+\frac{w+1}2\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u,
28	\]
29	and letting $T\to\infty$ for $\re w>1$ yields \eqref{eq:zeta-B2}. The last integral and its $w$-derivatives are dominated on $\re w\ge\eta>-1$ by $(\log u)^mu^{-\eta-2}/6$, so the integral is holomorphic for $\re w>-1$. At $w=0$ the formula gives $-1+\frac12=-\frac12$. At $w=-\frac12$ it gives $\zeta(-\frac12)=-\frac5{24}+\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-3/2}\dd u$, and the integral has modulus at most $\frac16\cdot2=\frac13$.
30	\end{proof}
31	
32	\section{The local factors}
33	
34	For each prime $p$ put
35	\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd}
36	\alpha_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
37	\beta_p=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
38	\delta_p=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
39	\end{equation}
40	By \eqref{eq:W-intro}, $w_p(h)$ equals $\alpha_p$, $\alpha_p+\beta_p$ or $\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p$ according as $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. By \cref{lem:rho} (with $C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|\}$),
41	\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd-bounds}
42	1-\frac2{p^2}\le\alpha_p\le1,\quad0\le\beta_p\le\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}\le\frac{C_0}{p^3},\quad0\le\delta_p\le\frac1{p^2},\quad\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-\frac1{p^2}.
43	\end{equation}
44	Here $\beta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)$, $\delta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p)\le p$, and $\alpha_p\le1$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p^2$. Define
45	\begin{equation}\label{eq:LM}
46	L_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s},\qquad
47	M_p(s)=\bigl(1-p^{-2s-2}\bigr)L_p(s),
48	\end{equation}
49	and $P_f(s)=\prod_pL_p(s)$, $H_f(s)=\prod_pM_p(s)$. In the notation of the archived proposition, $L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})B_p(s)$ with $B_p(s)=a_p+(b_p-a_p)p^{-s}+(c_p-b_p)p^{-2s}$, $a_p=1+\rho(p^2)/(p^2(p^2-2))$, $b_p=1+\rho(p)/(p(p^2-2))$, $c_p=1+1/(p^2-2)$. Expanding the product, with $z=p^{-s}$,
50	\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-expand}
51	M_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\bigl(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}\bigr)z^2-\beta_pp^{-2}z^3-\delta_pp^{-2}z^4,\qquad
52	\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}=-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6}.
53	\end{equation}
54	The cancellation of the terms $\pm p^{-2}$ in the coefficient of $z^2$ is what allows $H_f$ to converge beyond $\re s=-\frac12$.
55	
56	\section{The factorisation}
57	
58	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:Df}
59	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
60	\item The series $D_f(s)=\sum_hW_f(h)h^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\re s>1$.
61	\item The products $P_f$ and $H_f$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, and define holomorphic functions, on $\re s>-\frac12$ and $\re s>-\frac34$ respectively. For every fixed $\sigma>-\frac34$ there is $C(f,\sigma)$ with $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le C(f,\sigma)$ for all real $t$.
62	\item For $\re s>1$, $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. The function $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ continues $D_f$ meromorphically to $\re s>-\frac34$, and its only possible poles there are simple poles at $s=1$ and $s=-\frac12$.
63	\item $R_f=\Res_{s=1}D_f(s)=P_f(1)$. Moreover $R_f=\widetilde R_f$, where $\widetilde R_f$ is the series of \cref{lem:W-basic}, and \eqref{eq:R-intro} holds. Moreover $B_f=(\gamma_E-\frac32)R_f+P_f'(1)$, and $R_f>0$.
64	\item $D_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}=-\frac c2$.
65	\item We have $\Res_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)=\frac12\zeta(-\frac12)H_f(-\frac12)$, and hence
66	\[
67	K_f=-\tfrac83\,\zeta(-\tfrac12)\,H_f(-\tfrac12).
68	\]
69	Moreover $H_f(-\frac12)>0$ and $K_f>0$, and $K_f$ is given by the absolutely convergent product \eqref{eq:K-intro}.
70	\end{enumerate}
71	\end{proposition}

73	\begin{proof}
74	(a) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $0<W_f(h)\le1$, so $\sum_h|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_hh^{-\re s}$.
75	
76	(b) For $\re s\ge\sigma$, \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} gives $|L_p(s)-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}$. If $\sigma>-\frac12$ all exponents exceed one, so by \cref{lem:sums}(c) the sum over $p$ converges uniformly on $\re s\ge\sigma$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. For $M_p$, \eqref{eq:M-expand} and \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} give, for $\re s\ge\sigma$,
77	\[
78	|M_p(s)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}+\frac{C_0}{p^{3+\sigma}}+\Bigl(\frac{C_0}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}+\frac{C_0}{p^5}\Bigr)p^{-2\sigma}+\frac{C_0}{p^{5+3\sigma}}+\frac1{p^{4+4\sigma}}.
79	\]
80	For $\sigma>-\frac34$ the exponents $2$, $3+\sigma$, $3+2\sigma$, $4+2\sigma$, $5+2\sigma$, $5+3\sigma$ and $4+4\sigma$ all exceed one. Hence $\sum_p\sup_{\re s\ge\sigma}|M_p(s)-1|=:E_H(\sigma)<\infty$, and \cref{lem:products} gives absolute and locally uniform convergence, holomorphy, and $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(E_H(\sigma))$ for all $t$.
81	
82	(c) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p>0$, and $u(h)=W_f(h)/W_f(1)$ is multiplicative with $u(p)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p)/\alpha_p$ and $u(p^e)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p)/\alpha_p$ for $e\ge2$. For $\re s>1$ and $z=p^{-s}$ its local series is
83	\[
84	1+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p}{\alpha_p}z+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p}{\alpha_p}\cdot\frac{z^2}{1-z}=\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\delta_pz^2}{\alpha_p(1-z)}=\frac{L_p(s)}{\alpha_p(1-p^{-s})}.
85	\]
86	Since $\sum_h|u(h)h^{-s}|<\infty$, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\sum_hu(h)h^{-s}=\prod_pL_p(s)\alpha_p^{-1}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$. Multiplying by the convergent product $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p$ and using the Euler product of $\zeta$ gives $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)$; the limits of partial products multiply. For $\re s>-\frac12$ we have $\re(2s+2)>1$, so $\prod_p(1-p^{-2s-2})^{-1}=\zeta(2s+2)$ converges absolutely, and multiplying the products gives $P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. By \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $\zeta(s)$ and $\zeta(2s+2)$ are meromorphic for $\re s>-\frac34$, since then $\re s>-1$ and $\re(2s+2)>\frac12$. Their only poles there are at $s=1$ and at $2s+2=1$, both simple. Since $H_f$ is holomorphic, $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ is the required continuation.
87	
88	(d) Since $P_f$ is holomorphic near $1$ and $\zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+O(s-1)$ by \cref{lem:zeta}(a), we have $D_f(s)=\frac{P_f(1)}{s-1}+\gamma_EP_f(1)+P_f'(1)+O(s-1)$. This gives $R_f=P_f(1)$ and the formula for $B_f$ from \eqref{eq:RBK}. Substituting \eqref{eq:abd},
89	\[
90	L_p(1)=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}p+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}
91	=\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\bigl(1+T_p\bigr),
92	\]
93	with $T_p=(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))/(p^2-1)^2\ge0$. By \cref{lem:rho}(d) and $p^2-1\ge\frac34p^2$, $T_p\le\frac{16C_0}9(p^{-3}+p^{-4})$, which is summable. Using \eqref{eq:c-euler}, $R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p(1+T_p)>0$, which is \eqref{eq:R-intro}. For the identification with $\widetilde R_f$, note that $\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=c^2v(r)$, where $v$ is the nonnegative multiplicative function supported on cube-free integers with
94	\[
95	v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad v(p^2)=\frac{\varphi(p^2)\rho(p^2)}{p^2(p^2-1)^2}=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2},
96	\]
97	using \cref{lem:rho}(a) for multiplicativity of $\rho$. Thus $1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p$. Since $\sum_rv(r)<\infty$ by \cref{lem:W-basic}, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\widetilde R_f=c^2\prod_p(1+T_p)=R_f$.
98	
99	(e) $L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}$, so $P_f(0)=c$ by \eqref{eq:c-euler}. The identity $D_f=\zeta P_f$ persists on $\re s>-\frac12$ by (c), and both factors are regular at $0$; by \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $D_f(0)=\zeta(0)c=-c/2$.
100	
101	(f) Near $s=-\frac12$, $\zeta(2s+2)=\frac{1/2}{s+1/2}+O(1)$, while $\zeta(s)$ and $H_f(s)$ are holomorphic. This gives the residue, and the formula for $K_f$ follows from \eqref{eq:RBK}. At $s=-\frac12$,
102	\[
103	M_p(-\tfrac12)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\Bigl(1+\frac1p-\frac{2+\rho(p)}{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p)}{p^{5/2}}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^{7/2}}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4}\Bigr),
104	\]
105	by direct substitution of \eqref{eq:abd}. This is positive because $\alpha_p>0$ and $\beta_p,\delta_p\ge0$. The deviations $|M_p(-\frac12)-1|$ are summable by (b), so \cref{lem:products}(c) gives $H_f(-\frac12)>0$, and \cref{lem:zeta}(b) gives $\zeta(-\frac12)<0$. Hence $K_f>0$, and \eqref{eq:K-intro} is the product $H_f(-\frac12)=\prod_pM_p(-\frac12)$, with the factors at each prime kept together.
106	\end{proof}

108	\begin{remark}
109	Both poles in (c) are genuine, since $R_f>0$ and $K_f>0$. The value $D_f(0)=-c/2$ is essential: in \cref{ch:mellin} it produces the term $+cH$ in the expansion of $\Theta_f(H)$, which cancels the diagonal term $cx(Y-Z)$ of \cref{prop:reduction}. The identity $R_f=\widetilde R_f$ makes the logarithmic terms cancel as well.
110	\end{remark}

1	Put \(A_d=[t^d]f(t)\ne0\), and fix
2	\[
3	C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|,1\}.
4	\]
5	For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
6	polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
7	roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
8	\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
9	exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
10	\[
11	0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
12	0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}
13	\]
14	These bounds require no assumption on the content, discriminant, or
15	factorization of \(f\).
16	
17	We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
18	\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
19	\[
20	\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
21	\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
22	=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
23	\]
24	Both sums in (2) have infinitely many possible indices. A bound
25	\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
26	\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
27	all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).
28	If local factors are \(1+e_p(s)\), the estimate
29	\[
30	\left|\prod_{p>N}(1+e_p(s))-1\right|
31	\le \exp\!\left(\sum_{p>N}|e_p(s)|\right)-1          \tag{3}
32	\]
33	follows first for finite products by expansion and then for their limits.
34	Thus all the prime-sum tail estimates below also give explicit product
35	tail estimates. Uniform summability of \(|e_p|\) on compact sets gives
36	local uniform convergence to a holomorphic function, since the finite
37	products are holomorphic.
38	
39	For brevity put \(q_p=1-2/p^2\), and introduce the three coefficients
40	\[
41	\begin{aligned}
42	\alpha_p&=q_pa_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
43	\beta_p&=q_p(b_p-a_p)=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}
44	                              -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
45	\delta_p&=q_p(c_p-b_p)=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
46	\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
47	\]
48	By (1),
49	\[
50	\begin{gathered}
51	0<q_p\le\alpha_p\le1,\qquad
52	0\le\beta_p\le C_0p^{-3},\qquad
53	0\le\delta_p\le p^{-2},\\
54	|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3},\qquad
55	\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}.                 \tag{5}
56	\end{gathered}
57	\]
58	In particular, \(b_p-a_p\ge0\) and \(c_p-b_p\ge0\).
59	
60	The local factor \(w_p(h)\) in \(W_f(h)\) is, according as
61	\(v_p(h)=0,1\) or at least \(2\),
62	\[
63	w_p(h)=\alpha_p,\quad
64	\alpha_p+\beta_p,\quad
65	\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p,
66	\]
67	respectively. Alternatively, the elementary bound
68	\(0\le\rho(p^j)\le p^j\), including \(j=0\), gives directly
69	\[
70	1-\frac2{p^2}\le w_p(h)\le1-\frac1{p^2},\qquad
71	|w_p(h)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}.                          \tag{6}
72	\]
73	The prime tail of the last bound is at most \(2/N\) by (2), uniformly
74	in \(h\). Every factor is at least \(1/2\). For \(1/2\le t\le1\),
75	\(-\log t\le2(1-t)\); hence
76	\[
77	\sum_p|\log w_p(h)|\le4\sum_pp^{-2}\le4.
78	\]
79	It follows that the product defining \(W_f(h)\) is absolutely convergent
80	and \(0<W_f(h)\le1\). For \(s=\sigma+it\) with \(\sigma>1\), this gives
81	\[
82	\sum_{h\ge1}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_{h\ge1}h^{-\sigma}<\infty.
83	\]
84	More explicitly, the sum of the errors over the infinitely many indices
85	\(h>N\) is bounded by
86	\[
87	\sum_{h>N}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|
88	\le\sum_{h>N}h^{-\sigma}
89	\le\frac{N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                  \tag{7}
90	\]
91	This proves the asserted absolute convergence of \(D_f\).

93	Write
94	\[
95	L_p(s)=q_pB_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s}.
96	\]
97	On the closed half-plane \(\Re s\ge\sigma\), (5) gives the bound for
98	each individual prime
99	\[
100	|L_p(s)-1|
101	\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}.       \tag{8}
102	\]
103	If \(\sigma>-1/2\), all four exponents exceed \(1\). Summing (8) over
104	the infinitely many primes \(p>N\), using (2) separately for its four
105	terms, yields
106	\[
107	\begin{aligned}
108	\sum_{p>N}|L_p(s)-1|\le E_P(N;\sigma)
109	={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
110	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
111	 +\frac{N^{-1-2\sigma}}{1+2\sigma}.                 \tag{9}
112	\end{aligned}
113	\]
114	Every power of \(N\) on the right has negative exponent. Equations
115	(3) and (9) prove absolute and locally uniform convergence of \(P_f\)
116	on \(\Re s>-1/2\). They also prove its holomorphy there.
117	
118	The local factor in \(H_f\) is
119	\[
120	\begin{aligned}
121	M_p(s)&=(1-p^{-2s-2})L_p(s)\\
122	 &=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}
123	 +(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2})p^{-2s}
124	 -\beta_pp^{-2}p^{-3s}-\delta_pp^{-2}p^{-4s}.         \tag{10}
125	\end{aligned}
126	\]
127	The coefficient where cancellation is needed is exactly
128	\[
129	\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}
130	 =-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}
131	                         -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6},
132	\]
133	so its absolute value is at most
134	\(C_0p^{-3}+2p^{-4}+C_0p^{-5}\). Thus, for \(\Re s\ge\sigma\),
135	\[
136	\begin{aligned}
137	|M_p(s)-1|\le{}&2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}
138	 +C_0p^{-3-2\sigma}+2p^{-4-2\sigma}\\
139	 &+C_0p^{-5-2\sigma}+C_0p^{-5-3\sigma}
140	 +p^{-4-4\sigma}.                                  \tag{11}
141	\end{aligned}
142	\]
143	For \(\sigma>-3/4\), the eight exponents on the right are, respectively,
144	\[
145	2,\ 3,\ 3+\sigma,\ 3+2\sigma,\ 4+2\sigma,
146	\ 5+2\sigma,\ 5+3\sigma,\ 4+4\sigma,
147	\]
148	and each is greater than \(1\). The sum over the infinitely many primes
149	\(p>N\), before summation bounded prime by prime by (11), is after
150	summation bounded by
151	\[
152	\begin{aligned}
153	\sum_{p>N}|M_p(s)-1|\le E_H(N;\sigma)
154	={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
155	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
156	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-2\sigma}}{2+2\sigma}\\
157	 &+\frac{2N^{-3-2\sigma}}{3+2\sigma}
158	 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-2\sigma}}{4+2\sigma}
159	 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-3\sigma}}{4+3\sigma}
160	 +\frac{N^{-3-4\sigma}}{3+4\sigma}.                 \tag{12}
161	\end{aligned}
162	\]
163	All denominators in (12) are positive, and all powers of \(N\) have
164	negative exponents in this range. Equations (3) and (12) prove absolute
165	and locally uniform convergence, and holomorphy, of \(H_f\) on
166	\(\Re s>-3/4\). For every real \(t\), the bound
167	\(|M_p(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(|M_p(\sigma+it)-1|)\) also proves
168	\[
169	|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le \exp(E_H(1;\sigma)).             \tag{13}
170	\]
171	Thus one may take \(C(f,\sigma)=\exp(E_H(1;\sigma))\), with every
172	term in its exponent specified in (12).

174	We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
175	\[
176	A=\prod_p\alpha_p
177	\]
178	exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
179	\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
180	this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
181	\[
182	u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
183	u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).
184	\]
185	In particular \(0<u(h)\le A^{-1}\). For \(\Re s>1\), its local series is
186	\[
187	\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}
188	 =1+\frac{b_p}{a_p}p^{-s}
189	       +\frac{c_p}{a_p}\frac{p^{-2s}}{1-p^{-s}}
190	 =\frac{B_p(s)}{a_p(1-p^{-s})}.                    \tag{14}
191	\]
192	To justify multiplication of these series, first include only primes
193	\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers
194	whose prime factors are all at most \(N\). Every omitted integer is
195	greater than \(N\). The omitted sum has infinitely many possible
196	indices, each term has modulus at most \(A^{-1}h^{-\sigma}\), and its
197	total modulus is at most
198	\[
199	\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}
200	\]
201	This tends to zero. Multiplying (14) over all primes therefore gives
202	\[
203	\begin{aligned}
204	D_f(s)
205	 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}
206	 \left(\prod_{p\le N}\frac{L_p(s)}{1-p^{-s}}\right)
207	 \left(\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p\right)\\
208	 &=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad \Re s>1.                 \tag{16}
209	\end{aligned}
210	\]
211	Here the Euler product for \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\) follows
212	by unique prime factorization: its finite-prime expansion omits only
213	integers \(n>N\), whose total absolute contribution is at most
214	\(N^{1-\sigma}/(\sigma-1)\). The extra tail product in (16) tends to
215	\(1\), with explicit bound
216	\[
217	\left|\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p-1\right|
218	 \le \exp\!\left(\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}\right)-1. \tag{17}
219	\]

221	For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
222	absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since
223	\(|p^{-2s-2}|<1\) and
224	\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent
225	products defining \(P_f\) and \(H_f\) gives
226	\[
227	P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\quad(\Re s>-1/2).          \tag{18}
228	\]
229	In particular, (16) proves both required identities on \(\Re s>1\).

231	For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
232	signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
233	counting function of the positive integers gives
234	\[
235	\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
236	 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
237	       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
238	\]
239	Let
240	\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
241	This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
242	by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
243	integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
244	parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
245	exact identity
246	\[
247	\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
248	 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
249	  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
250	\]
251	The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
252	term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
253	\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
254	Substitution in (19) therefore yields
255	\[
256	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
257	 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
258	       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
259	\]
260	The integral is holomorphic for \(\Re w>-1\). Explicitly, its tail
261	past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
262	at most
263	\[
264	\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
265	\]
266	For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
267	integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)
268	by \((\log x)^m x^{-\eta-2}/6\), whose integral is
269	\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the
270	continuation in (20), with its sole pole at \(w=1\) and residue \(1\).
271	
272	We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),
273	the same counting-function integration gives, initially for
274	\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
275	\[
276	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}
277	       -w\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-w-1}\,dx.           \tag{22}
278	\]
279	The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms. The final integral, including
280	its coefficient, is bounded by
281	\(|w|N^{-\Re w}/\Re w\). Subtracting \(1/(w-1)\) and taking
282	\(w\to1\) gives
283	\[
284	\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
285	 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N
286	       -\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-2}\,dx.
287	\]
288	The integral is between \(0\) and \(1/N\). Taking \(N\to\infty\),
289	the right side is Euler's constant \(\gamma_E\), by its defining
290	harmonic-sum limit.
291	
292	Equation (20) gives \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\). At \(w=-1/2\) it gives
293	\[
294	\zeta(-1/2)=-\frac5{24}
295	       +\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-3/2}\,dx.
296	\]
297	The integral has absolute value at most
298	\((1/6)\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx=1/3\). Hence
299	\[
300	-\frac14\le\zeta(-1/2)\le-\frac16<0.              \tag{23}
301	\]
302	
303	For \(\Re s>-3/4\), the two arguments \(s\) and \(2s+2\) in
304	\[
305	\widetilde D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)         \tag{24}
306	\]
307	satisfy \(\Re s>-1\) and \(\Re(2s+2)>1/2>-1\).
308	Thus (20) and the holomorphy of \(H_f\) prove that (24) is
309	meromorphic throughout this region. It agrees with \(D_f\) on
310	\(\Re s>1\) by (16) and (18), so it is the claimed continuation.
311	We henceforth use the notation \(D_f\) for this continuation.
312	
313	At \(s=0\),
314	\[
315	L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2},\qquad
316	P_f(0)=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=\frac1{\zeta(2)}.
317	\]
318	The equality \(D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)\) extends meromorphically to
319	\(\Re s>-1/2\) by (18) and (24). Both factors are regular at zero,
320	so
321	\[
322	D_f(0)=\zeta(0)P_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}.          \tag{25}
323	\]
324	
325	At \(s=1\), \(P_f\) is holomorphic. With \(R_f=P_f(1)\), equations
326	(16) and (22) show
327	\[
328	\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)=R_f,\qquad
329	\lim_{s\to1}\left(D_f(s)-\frac{R_f}{s-1}\right)
330	 =\gamma_ER_f+P_f'(1)=B_f+\frac32R_f.               \tag{26}
331	\]
332	This proves that the definitions of \(R_f\) and \(B_f\) have the
333	specified values without any unspecified remainder in a Laurent
334	expansion.
335	
336	At \(s=-1/2\), every local factor of \(H_f\) is strictly positive:
337	\[
338	M_p(-1/2)
339	 =(1-p^{-1})\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)>0. \tag{27}
340	\]
341	The nonnegativity and strict positivity needed here are exactly (5).
342	The series of absolute deviations of these factors from \(1\)
343	converges by (11)--(12) with \(\sigma=-1/2\). A convergent product
344	of positive factors with summable absolute deviations has positive
345	limit: after finitely many factors, \(|M_p(-1/2)-1|\le1/2\), and
346	then \(|\log M_p(-1/2)|\le2|M_p(-1/2)-1|\).
347	Consequently \(H_f(-1/2)>0\). Combining this with (23) proves
348	\[
349	K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.                \tag{28}
350	\]
351	For clarity, the explicit Euler product in this constant is
352	\[
353	K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)
354	 \prod_p\left\{
355	 (1-2/p^2)(1-1/p)
356	 \bigl[a_p+(b_p-a_p)\sqrt p+(c_p-b_p)p\bigr]
357	 \right\}.                                       \tag{29}
358	\]
359	The factors inside braces are kept grouped at each prime; their
360	absolute convergence is precisely the convergence just proved for
361	\(H_f(-1/2)\). The pole of \(\zeta(2s+2)\) contributes a factor
362	\(1/2\) to its residue. Equations (23)--(24) therefore also give
363	\[
364	\operatorname*{Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
365	 =\frac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)=-\frac3{16}K_f.       \tag{30}
366	\]
367	The only possible poles in the stated region are \(1\) and \(-1/2\).
368	Both are genuine: the local factors of \(P_f(1)\) are positive with
369	summable absolute deviations, and (28) makes (30) nonzero.
370	
371	It remains to identify the common density coefficient. Substitution
372	of (4) into \(L_p(1)\) gives the exact identity
373	\[
374	\begin{aligned}
375	L_p(1)
376	 &=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}{p}+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}\\
377	 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}
378	       +\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}\\
379	 &=(1-p^{-2})^2
380	 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right].
381	                                                               \tag{31}
382	\end{aligned}
383	\]
384	Let
385	\[
386	T_p=\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}.
387	\]
388	Since \(p^2-1\ge3p^2/4\), (1) bounds the term for each prime by
389	\[
390	0\le T_p\le\frac{16C_0}{9}(p^{-4}+p^{-3}).          \tag{32}
391	\]
392	The sum over the infinitely many primes \(p>N\) is therefore bounded
393	explicitly by
394	\[
395	\sum_{p>N}T_p
396	 \le\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right). \tag{33}
397	\]
398	This proves absolute convergence of the product of \(1+T_p\).
399	The product of \((1-p^{-2})^2\) is absolutely convergent as well,
400	since the absolute deviation of its factor from \(1\) is
401	\(2p^{-2}-p^{-4}\le2p^{-2}\), with prime tail at most \(2/N\).
402	Multiplying (31) over the primes and using the Euler product for
403	\(\zeta(2)\) proves
404	\[
405	R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p
406	 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right]. \tag{34}
407	\]
408	
409	Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
410	\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between
411	residues modulo \(mn\) and pairs of residues modulo \(m,n\) restricts
412	to a bijection between the respective polynomial roots. Put
413	\[
414	v(r)=
415	\begin{cases}
416	\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(r)\rho(r)}r
417	             \prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2},
418	 &\text{if no prime cube divides }r,\\
419	0,&\text{otherwise}.
420	\end{cases}
421	\]
422	This is a nonnegative multiplicative function with \(v(1)=1\).
423	Its first two prime-power values are
424	\[
425	v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
426	v(p^2)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2}.          \tag{35}
427	\]
428	For \(e\ge3\), its value \(v(p^e)\) is zero.
429	For the primes at most \(N\), the finite product of
430	\(1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p\) expands into a finite nonnegative sum over
431	the \(3^{\pi(N)}\) integers obtained by choosing each such prime's
432	exponent from \(\{0,1,2\}\). These sets increase to all integers
433	with no prime-cube divisor. By (32) and (2), their sums are bounded
434	by
435	\[
436	\prod_p(1+T_p)\le
437	 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)\right)
438	 =\exp(40C_0/27).                                  \tag{36}
439	\]
440	Monotone convergence thus proves absolute convergence and the
441	Euler-product identity
442	\[
443	\sum_{r\ge1}v(r)=\prod_p(1+T_p).
444	\]
445	Explicitly, the omitted sum over the infinitely many integers having
446	a prime divisor greater than \(N\) is at most
447	\[
448	\exp(40C_0/27)
449	 \left[
450	 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}
451	                \left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right)\right)-1
452	 \right].                                         \tag{37}
453	\]
454	Indeed the omitted sum is exactly
455	\[
456	\left(\prod_{p\le N}(1+T_p)\right)
457	\left(\prod_{p>N}(1+T_p)-1\right),
458	\]
459	so (3), (33), and (36) give (37).
460	The definition of \(\lambda(r)\) in the statement satisfies
461	\(\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=\zeta(2)^{-2}v(r)\). Equations (34)--(35)
462	therefore give the required identity
463	\[
464	R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
465	\]
466	All the Euler products specifying \(R_f\) or \(K_f\) have had their
467	absolute convergence established above.
468	
469	No external literature or numerical checks were used in this proof.
470
