Put \(A_d=[t^d]f(t)\ne0\), and fix
\[
C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|,1\}.
\]
For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
\[
0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}
\]
These bounds require no assumption on the content, discriminant, or
factorization of \(f\).

We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
\[
\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
\]
Both sums in (2) have infinitely many possible indices. A bound
\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).
If local factors are \(1+e_p(s)\), the estimate
\[
\left|\prod_{p>N}(1+e_p(s))-1\right|
\le \exp\!\left(\sum_{p>N}|e_p(s)|\right)-1          \tag{3}
\]
follows first for finite products by expansion and then for their limits.
Thus all the prime-sum tail estimates below also give explicit product
tail estimates. Uniform summability of \(|e_p|\) on compact sets gives
local uniform convergence to a holomorphic function, since the finite
products are holomorphic.

For brevity put \(q_p=1-2/p^2\), and introduce the three coefficients
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_p&=q_pa_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
\beta_p&=q_p(b_p-a_p)=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}
                              -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
\delta_p&=q_p(c_p-b_p)=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
\]
By (1),
\[
\begin{gathered}
0<q_p\le\alpha_p\le1,\qquad
0\le\beta_p\le C_0p^{-3},\qquad
0\le\delta_p\le p^{-2},\\
|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3},\qquad
\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}.                 \tag{5}
\end{gathered}
\]
In particular, \(b_p-a_p\ge0\) and \(c_p-b_p\ge0\).

The local factor \(w_p(h)\) in \(W_f(h)\) is, according as
\(v_p(h)=0,1\) or at least \(2\),
\[
w_p(h)=\alpha_p,\quad
\alpha_p+\beta_p,\quad
\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p,
\]
respectively. Alternatively, the elementary bound
\(0\le\rho(p^j)\le p^j\), including \(j=0\), gives directly
\[
1-\frac2{p^2}\le w_p(h)\le1-\frac1{p^2},\qquad
|w_p(h)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}.                          \tag{6}
\]
The prime tail of the last bound is at most \(2/N\) by (2), uniformly
in \(h\). Every factor is at least \(1/2\). For \(1/2\le t\le1\),
\(-\log t\le2(1-t)\); hence
\[
\sum_p|\log w_p(h)|\le4\sum_pp^{-2}\le4.
\]
It follows that the product defining \(W_f(h)\) is absolutely convergent
and \(0<W_f(h)\le1\). For \(s=\sigma+it\) with \(\sigma>1\), this gives
\[
\sum_{h\ge1}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_{h\ge1}h^{-\sigma}<\infty.
\]
More explicitly, the sum of the errors over the infinitely many indices
\(h>N\) is bounded by
\[
\sum_{h>N}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|
\le\sum_{h>N}h^{-\sigma}
\le\frac{N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                  \tag{7}
\]
This proves the asserted absolute convergence of \(D_f\).

Write
\[
L_p(s)=q_pB_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s}.
\]
On the closed half-plane \(\Re s\ge\sigma\), (5) gives the bound for
each individual prime
\[
|L_p(s)-1|
\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}.       \tag{8}
\]
If \(\sigma>-1/2\), all four exponents exceed \(1\). Summing (8) over
the infinitely many primes \(p>N\), using (2) separately for its four
terms, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{p>N}|L_p(s)-1|\le E_P(N;\sigma)
={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
 +\frac{N^{-1-2\sigma}}{1+2\sigma}.                 \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Every power of \(N\) on the right has negative exponent. Equations
(3) and (9) prove absolute and locally uniform convergence of \(P_f\)
on \(\Re s>-1/2\). They also prove its holomorphy there.

The local factor in \(H_f\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_p(s)&=(1-p^{-2s-2})L_p(s)\\
 &=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}
 +(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2})p^{-2s}
 -\beta_pp^{-2}p^{-3s}-\delta_pp^{-2}p^{-4s}.         \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient where cancellation is needed is exactly
\[
\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}
 =-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}
                         -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6},
\]
so its absolute value is at most
\(C_0p^{-3}+2p^{-4}+C_0p^{-5}\). Thus, for \(\Re s\ge\sigma\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|M_p(s)-1|\le{}&2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}
 +C_0p^{-3-2\sigma}+2p^{-4-2\sigma}\\
 &+C_0p^{-5-2\sigma}+C_0p^{-5-3\sigma}
 +p^{-4-4\sigma}.                                  \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\sigma>-3/4\), the eight exponents on the right are, respectively,
\[
2,\ 3,\ 3+\sigma,\ 3+2\sigma,\ 4+2\sigma,
\ 5+2\sigma,\ 5+3\sigma,\ 4+4\sigma,
\]
and each is greater than \(1\). The sum over the infinitely many primes
\(p>N\), before summation bounded prime by prime by (11), is after
summation bounded by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{p>N}|M_p(s)-1|\le E_H(N;\sigma)
={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-2\sigma}}{2+2\sigma}\\
 &+\frac{2N^{-3-2\sigma}}{3+2\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-2\sigma}}{4+2\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-3\sigma}}{4+3\sigma}
 +\frac{N^{-3-4\sigma}}{3+4\sigma}.                 \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
All denominators in (12) are positive, and all powers of \(N\) have
negative exponents in this range. Equations (3) and (12) prove absolute
and locally uniform convergence, and holomorphy, of \(H_f\) on
\(\Re s>-3/4\). For every real \(t\), the bound
\(|M_p(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(|M_p(\sigma+it)-1|)\) also proves
\[
|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le \exp(E_H(1;\sigma)).             \tag{13}
\]
Thus one may take \(C(f,\sigma)=\exp(E_H(1;\sigma))\), with every
term in its exponent specified in (12).

We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
\[
A=\prod_p\alpha_p
\]
exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
\[
u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).
\]
In particular \(0<u(h)\le A^{-1}\). For \(\Re s>1\), its local series is
\[
\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}
 =1+\frac{b_p}{a_p}p^{-s}
       +\frac{c_p}{a_p}\frac{p^{-2s}}{1-p^{-s}}
 =\frac{B_p(s)}{a_p(1-p^{-s})}.                    \tag{14}
\]
To justify multiplication of these series, first include only primes
\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers
whose prime factors are all at most \(N\). Every omitted integer is
greater than \(N\). The omitted sum has infinitely many possible
indices, each term has modulus at most \(A^{-1}h^{-\sigma}\), and its
total modulus is at most
\[
\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}
\]
This tends to zero. Multiplying (14) over all primes therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_f(s)
 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}
 \left(\prod_{p\le N}\frac{L_p(s)}{1-p^{-s}}\right)
 \left(\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p\right)\\
 &=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad \Re s>1.                 \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the Euler product for \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\) follows
by unique prime factorization: its finite-prime expansion omits only
integers \(n>N\), whose total absolute contribution is at most
\(N^{1-\sigma}/(\sigma-1)\). The extra tail product in (16) tends to
\(1\), with explicit bound
\[
\left|\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p-1\right|
 \le \exp\!\left(\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}\right)-1. \tag{17}
\]

For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since
\(|p^{-2s-2}|<1\) and
\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent
products defining \(P_f\) and \(H_f\) gives
\[
P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\quad(\Re s>-1/2).          \tag{18}
\]
In particular, (16) proves both required identities on \(\Re s>1\).

For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
counting function of the positive integers gives
\[
\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
\]
Let
\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
exact identity
\[
\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
\]
The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
Substitution in (19) therefore yields
\[
\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
\]
The integral is holomorphic for \(\Re w>-1\). Explicitly, its tail
past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
at most
\[
\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
\]
For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)
by \((\log x)^m x^{-\eta-2}/6\), whose integral is
\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the
continuation in (20), with its sole pole at \(w=1\) and residue \(1\).

We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),
the same counting-function integration gives, initially for
\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
\[
\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}
       -w\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-w-1}\,dx.           \tag{22}
\]
The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms. The final integral, including
its coefficient, is bounded by
\(|w|N^{-\Re w}/\Re w\). Subtracting \(1/(w-1)\) and taking
\(w\to1\) gives
\[
\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N
       -\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-2}\,dx.
\]
The integral is between \(0\) and \(1/N\). Taking \(N\to\infty\),
the right side is Euler's constant \(\gamma_E\), by its defining
harmonic-sum limit.

Equation (20) gives \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\). At \(w=-1/2\) it gives
\[
\zeta(-1/2)=-\frac5{24}
       +\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-3/2}\,dx.
\]
The integral has absolute value at most
\((1/6)\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx=1/3\). Hence
\[
-\frac14\le\zeta(-1/2)\le-\frac16<0.              \tag{23}
\]

For \(\Re s>-3/4\), the two arguments \(s\) and \(2s+2\) in
\[
\widetilde D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)         \tag{24}
\]
satisfy \(\Re s>-1\) and \(\Re(2s+2)>1/2>-1\).
Thus (20) and the holomorphy of \(H_f\) prove that (24) is
meromorphic throughout this region. It agrees with \(D_f\) on
\(\Re s>1\) by (16) and (18), so it is the claimed continuation.
We henceforth use the notation \(D_f\) for this continuation.

At \(s=0\),
\[
L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2},\qquad
P_f(0)=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=\frac1{\zeta(2)}.
\]
The equality \(D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)\) extends meromorphically to
\(\Re s>-1/2\) by (18) and (24). Both factors are regular at zero,
so
\[
D_f(0)=\zeta(0)P_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}.          \tag{25}
\]

At \(s=1\), \(P_f\) is holomorphic. With \(R_f=P_f(1)\), equations
(16) and (22) show
\[
\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)=R_f,\qquad
\lim_{s\to1}\left(D_f(s)-\frac{R_f}{s-1}\right)
 =\gamma_ER_f+P_f'(1)=B_f+\frac32R_f.               \tag{26}
\]
This proves that the definitions of \(R_f\) and \(B_f\) have the
specified values without any unspecified remainder in a Laurent
expansion.

At \(s=-1/2\), every local factor of \(H_f\) is strictly positive:
\[
M_p(-1/2)
 =(1-p^{-1})\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)>0. \tag{27}
\]
The nonnegativity and strict positivity needed here are exactly (5).
The series of absolute deviations of these factors from \(1\)
converges by (11)--(12) with \(\sigma=-1/2\). A convergent product
of positive factors with summable absolute deviations has positive
limit: after finitely many factors, \(|M_p(-1/2)-1|\le1/2\), and
then \(|\log M_p(-1/2)|\le2|M_p(-1/2)-1|\).
Consequently \(H_f(-1/2)>0\). Combining this with (23) proves
\[
K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.                \tag{28}
\]
For clarity, the explicit Euler product in this constant is
\[
K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)
 \prod_p\left\{
 (1-2/p^2)(1-1/p)
 \bigl[a_p+(b_p-a_p)\sqrt p+(c_p-b_p)p\bigr]
 \right\}.                                       \tag{29}
\]
The factors inside braces are kept grouped at each prime; their
absolute convergence is precisely the convergence just proved for
\(H_f(-1/2)\). The pole of \(\zeta(2s+2)\) contributes a factor
\(1/2\) to its residue. Equations (23)--(24) therefore also give
\[
\operatorname*{Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
 =\frac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)=-\frac3{16}K_f.       \tag{30}
\]
The only possible poles in the stated region are \(1\) and \(-1/2\).
Both are genuine: the local factors of \(P_f(1)\) are positive with
summable absolute deviations, and (28) makes (30) nonzero.

It remains to identify the common density coefficient. Substitution
of (4) into \(L_p(1)\) gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_p(1)
 &=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}{p}+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}\\
 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}
       +\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}\\
 &=(1-p^{-2})^2
 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right].
                                                               \tag{31}
\end{aligned}
\]
Let
\[
T_p=\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}.
\]
Since \(p^2-1\ge3p^2/4\), (1) bounds the term for each prime by
\[
0\le T_p\le\frac{16C_0}{9}(p^{-4}+p^{-3}).          \tag{32}
\]
The sum over the infinitely many primes \(p>N\) is therefore bounded
explicitly by
\[
\sum_{p>N}T_p
 \le\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right). \tag{33}
\]
This proves absolute convergence of the product of \(1+T_p\).
The product of \((1-p^{-2})^2\) is absolutely convergent as well,
since the absolute deviation of its factor from \(1\) is
\(2p^{-2}-p^{-4}\le2p^{-2}\), with prime tail at most \(2/N\).
Multiplying (31) over the primes and using the Euler product for
\(\zeta(2)\) proves
\[
R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p
 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right]. \tag{34}
\]

Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between
residues modulo \(mn\) and pairs of residues modulo \(m,n\) restricts
to a bijection between the respective polynomial roots. Put
\[
v(r)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(r)\rho(r)}r
             \prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2},
 &\text{if no prime cube divides }r,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is a nonnegative multiplicative function with \(v(1)=1\).
Its first two prime-power values are
\[
v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
v(p^2)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2}.          \tag{35}
\]
For \(e\ge3\), its value \(v(p^e)\) is zero.
For the primes at most \(N\), the finite product of
\(1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p\) expands into a finite nonnegative sum over
the \(3^{\pi(N)}\) integers obtained by choosing each such prime's
exponent from \(\{0,1,2\}\). These sets increase to all integers
with no prime-cube divisor. By (32) and (2), their sums are bounded
by
\[
\prod_p(1+T_p)\le
 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)\right)
 =\exp(40C_0/27).                                  \tag{36}
\]
Monotone convergence thus proves absolute convergence and the
Euler-product identity
\[
\sum_{r\ge1}v(r)=\prod_p(1+T_p).
\]
Explicitly, the omitted sum over the infinitely many integers having
a prime divisor greater than \(N\) is at most
\[
\exp(40C_0/27)
 \left[
 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}
                \left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right)\right)-1
 \right].                                         \tag{37}
\]
Indeed the omitted sum is exactly
\[
\left(\prod_{p\le N}(1+T_p)\right)
\left(\prod_{p>N}(1+T_p)-1\right),
\]
so (3), (33), and (36) give (37).
The definition of \(\lambda(r)\) in the statement satisfies
\(\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=\zeta(2)^{-2}v(r)\). Equations (34)--(35)
therefore give the required identity
\[
R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
\]
All the Euler products specifying \(R_f\) or \(K_f\) have had their
absolute convergence established above.

No external literature or numerical checks were used in this proof.

1	# Proof of P6
2	
3	We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
4	`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
5	\[
6	D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
7	\tag{1}
8	\]
9	as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
10	\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
11	are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).
12	
13	## 1. The external statements used
14	
15	The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
16	*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
17	pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
18	as supplied in
19	`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
20	Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
21	typesetting transcribed from the PDF.
22	
23	> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
24	> \[
25	> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
26	> \tag{10.9}
27	> \]
28	
29	> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
30	> \[
31	> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
32	> \]
33	> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
34	> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.
35	
36	Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
37	For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
38	neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
39	strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
40	\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
41	part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
42	\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
43	and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
44	at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.
45	
46	For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
47	\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
48	\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
49	Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
50	\[
51	|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
52	\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
53	\tag{2}
54	\]
55	in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.
56	
57	## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip
58	
59	We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
60	on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
61	the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
62	\[
63	\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
64	       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
65	       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.
66	\tag{3}
67	\]
68	Indeed, write the tail as \(\int_N^\infty u^{-s}\,d\lfloor u\rfloor\),
69	replace \(\lfloor u\rfloor\) by \(u-\{u\}\), and integrate the second
70	term by parts. The boundary term at \(N\) vanishes because \(N\) is an
71	integer. The integral in (3) converges locally uniformly for
72	\(\Re s>0\), since \(0\leq\{u\}<1\); hence (3) holds there by analytic
73	continuation, away from \(s=1\). It also shows that the residue at one is
74	one and that there are no other poles in that half-plane.
75	
76	Let \(s=\alpha+iv\), \(V=|v|\geq2\),
77	\(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6\), and \(\delta\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Choose
78	\(N=\lceil V\rceil\), so \(V\leq N\leq3V/2\). The finite sum in (3)
79	has exactly \(N\) terms. Each term has modulus at most \(n^{-\delta}\),
80	and after summation its modulus is at most
81	\[
82	\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-\delta}
83	\leq1+\int_1^N u^{-\delta}\,du
84	\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}
85	\leq\frac{(3/2)^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}.
86	\]
87	The other two terms satisfy
88	\[
89	\left|\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}\right|
90	\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{V}
91	\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{-\delta}
92	\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}
93	\]
94	and
95	\[
96	\left|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du\right|
97	\leq\frac{|s|}{\alpha}N^{-\alpha}
98	\leq\frac{V+6}{\delta}V^{-\delta}
99	\leq\frac4\delta V^{1-\delta}.
100	\]
101	Consequently, with the explicit constants
102	\[
103	C_\delta=(3/2)^{1-\delta}
104	              \left(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\right)+\frac4\delta,
105	\]
106	we have
107	\[
108	|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\leq C_\delta V^{1-\delta}
109	\quad(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6,\ V\geq2).
110	\tag{4}
111	\]
112	
113	Now put \(s=\sigma+it\), \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2\), and \(T=|t|\geq2\).
114	For \(1/4\leq\sigma\leq2\), (4) with \(\delta=1/4\) gives
115	\[
116	|\zeta(s)|\leq C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\leq C_{1/4}T^{11/8}.
117	\]
118	For \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\), the real part of \(1-s\) lies in
119	\([3/4,13/8]\), so (4) with \(\delta=3/4\), followed by (2), gives
120	\[
121	\begin{aligned}
122	|\zeta(s)|
123	&\leq Q(T+4)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\\
124	&\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{3/4-\sigma}
125	\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}.
126	\end{aligned}
127	\]
128	Here \(T+4\leq3T\) and \(1/4\leq1/2-\sigma\leq9/8\).
129	Also \(3/4\leq\Re(2s+2)\leq6\), and its imaginary part has modulus
130	\(2T\geq4\). Thus
131	\[
132	|\zeta(2s+2)|\leq C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4}.
133	\tag{5}
134	\]
135	
136	We next obtain a bound for \(H_f(s)\) uniform on this whole strip.
137	This is a uniformity supplement to the fixed-line bound in P5; we do not
138	need to strengthen its domain of continuation. Write \(d=\deg f\), and
139	let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient
140	of \(f\). For \(p\notin\mathcal B\), its reduction is a nonzero
141	polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\), with at most \(d\) roots. Each residue
142	modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\), whence
143	\[
144	0\leq\rho(p)\leq d,\qquad0\leq\rho(p^2)\leq dp.
145	\tag{6}
146	\]
147	Use the quantities \(a_p,b_p,c_p\) defined in P5, and put
148	\(u_p=b_p-a_p\), \(q_p=c_p-b_p\). Since \(p^2-2\geq p^2/2\), (6)
149	gives
150	\[
151	\begin{gathered}
152	|a_p-1|\leq2dp^{-3},\qquad |u_p|\leq4dp^{-3},
153	\qquad |q_p|\leq(d+2)p^{-2},\\
154	|q_p-p^{-2}|\leq(2+2d)p^{-3},
155	\qquad |q_p-a_pp^{-2}|\leq(2+4d)p^{-3},\\
156	|(1-2p^{-2})a_p-1|\leq(2+4d)p^{-2}.
157	\end{gathered}
158	\tag{7}
159	\]
160	For the fourth inequality, the exact difference is
161	\[
162	q_p-p^{-2}=\frac{2-p\rho(p)}{p^2(p^2-2)},
163	\]
164	whose modulus is at most \(4p^{-4}+2dp^{-3}\leq(2+2d)p^{-3}\).
165	The fifth follows by adding \(|a_p-1|p^{-2}\leq2dp^{-5}\).
166	For the last inequality, the bound before collecting powers is
167	\(2dp^{-3}+2p^{-2}+4dp^{-5}\), which is at most the stated bound.
168	
169	Set \(z=p^{-s}\). The local factor of \(H_f\) is exactly
170	\[
171	L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})
172	 \left[a_p+u_pz+(q_p-a_pp^{-2})z^2
173	                    -u_pp^{-2}z^3-q_pp^{-2}z^4\right].
174	\]
175	Since \(|z|=p^{-\sigma}\leq p^{5/8}\), (7) implies
176	\[
177	\begin{aligned}
178	|L_p(s)-1|\leq{}& (2+4d)p^{-2}+4dp^{-19/8}
179	 +(2+4d)p^{-7/4}\\
180	&+4dp^{-25/8}+(d+2)p^{-3/2}
181	\leq(6+17d)p^{-3/2}.
182	\end{aligned}
183	\tag{8}
184	\]
185	The prime sum of these bounds is at most
186	\[
187	(6+17d)\sum_{n=2}^\infty n^{-3/2}
188	\leq(6+17d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
189	=2(6+17d).
190	\]
191	Thus the product over \(p\notin\mathcal B\) has modulus at most
192	\(\exp(2(6+17d))\). The remaining product has exactly
193	\(|\mathcal B|\) factors. Before multiplication each such factor is
194	bounded by the following finite number:
195	\[
196	U_p=(1-2p^{-2})(1+p^{-3/4})
197	       \left(|a_p|+|u_p|p^{5/8}+|q_p|p^{5/4}\right).
198	\]
199	After multiplication their modulus is at most
200	\(\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p\), with the empty product equal to one.
201	Therefore
202	\[
203	|H_f(s)|\leq M_H,
204	\qquad
205	M_H=\exp(2(6+17d))\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p,
206	\quad -5/8\leq\Re s\leq2.
207	\tag{9}
208	\]
209	Combining (1), (4), (5), and (9), define
210	\[
211	C_D=M_H\max\{C_{1/4},Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}\}
212	                    2^{1/4}C_{3/4}.
213	\]
214	We then have the explicit growth estimate
215	\[
216	|D_f(\sigma+it)|\leq C_D|t|^{13/8}
217	\quad(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2,\ |t|\geq2),
218	\tag{10}
219	\]
220	where the exponent is \(11/8+1/4=13/8\).
221	
222	## 3. Mellin representation and contour displacement
223	
224	The elementary kernel identity needed here is, for \(v>0\),
225	\[
226	\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
227	             \frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\,dz
228	=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\geq1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
229	\tag{11}
230	\]
231	For completeness, close a finite rectangle to the left when \(v\geq1\),
232	and to the right when \(v<1\). On a fixed horizontal segment at height
233	\(T\), the denominator has modulus at least \(T^3\), so those integrals
234	tend to zero as \(T\) tends to infinity. A new left edge
235	\(\Re z=-N-1/2\), \(N\geq3\), has normalized integral in modulus at most
236	\[
237	\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi}
238	\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
239	       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
240	=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
241	\]
242	because each of
243	\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
244	\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
245	A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
246	\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
247	are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
248	the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).
249	
250	Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
251	positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
252	\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
253	On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
254	\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
255	\[
256	\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
257	\]
258	Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
259	it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
260	segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
261	justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
262	\[
263	\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
264	\qquad
265	G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
266	\tag{12}
267	\]
268	The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
269	weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).
270	
271	Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
272	\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
273	\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
274	(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
275	checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
276	pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.
277	
278	Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
279	\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
280	least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
281	Thus (10) gives the bound
282	\[
283	|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
284	                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
285	\]
286	Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
287	over both segments, the bound is at most
288	\[
289	\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
290	\]
291	which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
292	asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.
293	
294	For that vertical line define the finite constant
295	\[
296	M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
297	\]
298	It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
299	(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
300	\[
301	|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
302	\]
303	The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
304	integrand is bounded by
305	\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
306	\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
307	tail, (10) gives
308	\[
309	|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
310	\qquad(|t|\geq2).
311	\]
312	After integration over both tails the bound is
313	\[
314	4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
315	=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.
316	\]
317	In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
318	\[
319	\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
320	                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
321	\leq C_*H^{3/8},
322	\tag{13}
323	\]
324	where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
325	\[
326	C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
327	       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
328	                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
329	\tag{14}
330	\]
331	The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
332	just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
333	left integral.
334	
335	## 4. Residues and the two estimates
336	
337	Write the Laurent expansion at one as
338	\[
339	D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
340	\]
341	Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
342	gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
343	about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
344	with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
345	by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
346	local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.
347	
348	Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
349	\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
350	\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
351	\[
352	H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
353	=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
354	\tag{15}
355	\]
356	At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
357	\[
358	\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
359	=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
360	\tag{16}
361	\]
362	At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
363	Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
364	\[
365	\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
366	=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
367	=-K_fH^{1/2}.
368	\tag{17}
369	\]
370	This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
371	\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
372	\[
373	-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
374	=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
375	\]
376	
377	Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
378	Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
379	\[
380	\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
381	\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
382	\tag{18}
383	\]
384	for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
385	an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
386	The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
387	the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
388	\[
389	F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
390	\]
391	Therefore
392	\[
393	|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
394	\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
395	\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
396	\]
397	which proves the second assertion with the same constant.
398	
399	## 5. The integral identity
400	
401	Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
402	\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
403	term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
404	\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
405	finite sum identity
406	\[
407	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
408	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
409	                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
410	\tag{19}
411	\]
412	For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
413	\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
414	\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
415	integral is exactly
416	\[
417	2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
418	=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
419	\tag{20}
420	\]
421	Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
422	\[
423	Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
424	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
425	\]
426	and
427	\[
428	Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
429	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
430	\]
431	In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
432	extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
433	zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
434	\[
435	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
436	=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
437	\]
438	This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.
439	
440	Exact symbolic checks in Python/SymPy verified the local-factor
441	expansion, the kernel coefficient at \(-1/2\), the kernel residue at
442	zero, and \(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). No numerical sanity check was
443	used. No excluded source or previous-run write-up was consulted, and no
444	objections file was supplied for this attempt.

# Proof of P6

We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
\[
D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
\tag{1}
\]
as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).

## 1. The external statements used

The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
as supplied in
`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
typesetting transcribed from the PDF.

> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
> \[
> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
> \tag{10.9}
> \]

> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
> \[
> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
> \]
> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.

Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.

For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
\[
|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
\tag{2}
\]
in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.

## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip

We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
\[
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, write the tail as \(\int_N^\infty u^{-s}\,d\lfloor u\rfloor\),
replace \(\lfloor u\rfloor\) by \(u-\{u\}\), and integrate the second
term by parts. The boundary term at \(N\) vanishes because \(N\) is an
integer. The integral in (3) converges locally uniformly for
\(\Re s>0\), since \(0\leq\{u\}<1\); hence (3) holds there by analytic
continuation, away from \(s=1\). It also shows that the residue at one is
one and that there are no other poles in that half-plane.

Let \(s=\alpha+iv\), \(V=|v|\geq2\),
\(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6\), and \(\delta\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Choose
\(N=\lceil V\rceil\), so \(V\leq N\leq3V/2\). The finite sum in (3)
has exactly \(N\) terms. Each term has modulus at most \(n^{-\delta}\),
and after summation its modulus is at most
\[
\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-\delta}
\leq1+\int_1^N u^{-\delta}\,du
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}
\leq\frac{(3/2)^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}.
\]
The other two terms satisfy
\[
\left|\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}\right|
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{V}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}
\]
and
\[
\left|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du\right|
\leq\frac{|s|}{\alpha}N^{-\alpha}
\leq\frac{V+6}{\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq\frac4\delta V^{1-\delta}.
\]
Consequently, with the explicit constants
\[
C_\delta=(3/2)^{1-\delta}
              \left(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\right)+\frac4\delta,
\]
we have
\[
|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\leq C_\delta V^{1-\delta}
\quad(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6,\ V\geq2).
\tag{4}
\]

Now put \(s=\sigma+it\), \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2\), and \(T=|t|\geq2\).
For \(1/4\leq\sigma\leq2\), (4) with \(\delta=1/4\) gives
\[
|\zeta(s)|\leq C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\leq C_{1/4}T^{11/8}.
\]
For \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\), the real part of \(1-s\) lies in
\([3/4,13/8]\), so (4) with \(\delta=3/4\), followed by (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\zeta(s)|
&\leq Q(T+4)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\\
&\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{3/4-\sigma}
\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(T+4\leq3T\) and \(1/4\leq1/2-\sigma\leq9/8\).
Also \(3/4\leq\Re(2s+2)\leq6\), and its imaginary part has modulus
\(2T\geq4\). Thus
\[
|\zeta(2s+2)|\leq C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4}.
\tag{5}
\]

We next obtain a bound for \(H_f(s)\) uniform on this whole strip.
This is a uniformity supplement to the fixed-line bound in P5; we do not
need to strengthen its domain of continuation. Write \(d=\deg f\), and
let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient
of \(f\). For \(p\notin\mathcal B\), its reduction is a nonzero
polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\), with at most \(d\) roots. Each residue
modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\), whence
\[
0\leq\rho(p)\leq d,\qquad0\leq\rho(p^2)\leq dp.
\tag{6}
\]
Use the quantities \(a_p,b_p,c_p\) defined in P5, and put
\(u_p=b_p-a_p\), \(q_p=c_p-b_p\). Since \(p^2-2\geq p^2/2\), (6)
gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
|a_p-1|\leq2dp^{-3},\qquad |u_p|\leq4dp^{-3},
\qquad |q_p|\leq(d+2)p^{-2},\\
|q_p-p^{-2}|\leq(2+2d)p^{-3},
\qquad |q_p-a_pp^{-2}|\leq(2+4d)p^{-3},\\
|(1-2p^{-2})a_p-1|\leq(2+4d)p^{-2}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{7}
\]
For the fourth inequality, the exact difference is
\[
q_p-p^{-2}=\frac{2-p\rho(p)}{p^2(p^2-2)},
\]
whose modulus is at most \(4p^{-4}+2dp^{-3}\leq(2+2d)p^{-3}\).
The fifth follows by adding \(|a_p-1|p^{-2}\leq2dp^{-5}\).
For the last inequality, the bound before collecting powers is
\(2dp^{-3}+2p^{-2}+4dp^{-5}\), which is at most the stated bound.

Set \(z=p^{-s}\). The local factor of \(H_f\) is exactly
\[
L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})
 \left[a_p+u_pz+(q_p-a_pp^{-2})z^2
                    -u_pp^{-2}z^3-q_pp^{-2}z^4\right].
\]
Since \(|z|=p^{-\sigma}\leq p^{5/8}\), (7) implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
|L_p(s)-1|\leq{}& (2+4d)p^{-2}+4dp^{-19/8}
 +(2+4d)p^{-7/4}\\
&+4dp^{-25/8}+(d+2)p^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)p^{-3/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
The prime sum of these bounds is at most
\[
(6+17d)\sum_{n=2}^\infty n^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
=2(6+17d).
\]
Thus the product over \(p\notin\mathcal B\) has modulus at most
\(\exp(2(6+17d))\). The remaining product has exactly
\(|\mathcal B|\) factors. Before multiplication each such factor is
bounded by the following finite number:
\[
U_p=(1-2p^{-2})(1+p^{-3/4})
       \left(|a_p|+|u_p|p^{5/8}+|q_p|p^{5/4}\right).
\]
After multiplication their modulus is at most
\(\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p\), with the empty product equal to one.
Therefore
\[
|H_f(s)|\leq M_H,
\qquad
M_H=\exp(2(6+17d))\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p,
\quad -5/8\leq\Re s\leq2.
\tag{9}
\]
Combining (1), (4), (5), and (9), define
\[
C_D=M_H\max\{C_{1/4},Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}\}
                    2^{1/4}C_{3/4}.
\]
We then have the explicit growth estimate
\[
|D_f(\sigma+it)|\leq C_D|t|^{13/8}
\quad(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2,\ |t|\geq2),
\tag{10}
\]
where the exponent is \(11/8+1/4=13/8\).

## 3. Mellin representation and contour displacement

The elementary kernel identity needed here is, for \(v>0\),
\[
\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
             \frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\,dz
=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\geq1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
\tag{11}
\]
For completeness, close a finite rectangle to the left when \(v\geq1\),
and to the right when \(v<1\). On a fixed horizontal segment at height
\(T\), the denominator has modulus at least \(T^3\), so those integrals
tend to zero as \(T\) tends to infinity. A new left edge
\(\Re z=-N-1/2\), \(N\geq3\), has normalized integral in modulus at most
\[
\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
\]
because each of
\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).

Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
\[
\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
\]
Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
\[
\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
\qquad
G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
\tag{12}
\]
The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).

Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.

Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
Thus (10) gives the bound
\[
|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
\]
Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
over both segments, the bound is at most
\[
\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
\]
which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.

For that vertical line define the finite constant
\[
M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
\]
It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
\[
|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
\]
The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
integrand is bounded by
\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
tail, (10) gives
\[
|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
\qquad(|t|\geq2).
\]
After integration over both tails the bound is
\[
4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.
\]
In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
\[
\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
\leq C_*H^{3/8},
\tag{13}
\]
where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
\[
C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
\tag{14}
\]
The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
left integral.

## 4. Residues and the two estimates

Write the Laurent expansion at one as
\[
D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
\]
Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.

Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
\[
H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
\tag{15}
\]
At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
\tag{16}
\]
At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-K_fH^{1/2}.
\tag{17}
\]
This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
\[
-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
\]

Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
\[
\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
\tag{18}
\]
for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
\[
F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
\]
which proves the second assertion with the same constant.

## 5. The integral identity

Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
finite sum identity
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
\tag{19}
\]
For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
integral is exactly
\[
2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
\tag{20}
\]
Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
\[
Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
\]
and
\[
Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
\]
In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\]
This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.

Exact symbolic checks in Python/SymPy verified the local-factor
expansion, the kernel coefficient at \(-1/2\), the kernel residue at
zero, and \(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). No numerical sanity check was
used. No excluded source or previous-run write-up was consulted, and no
objections file was supplied for this attempt.

1	\chapter{Proof of the main theorem}\label{ch:assembly}
2	
3	We now combine \cref{prop:reduction,prop:initial,prop:corr,prop:averaging,prop:Df,prop:Theta} and \cref{lem:integral-identity}. Throughout, $d=\deg f$,
4	\[
5	a=4d-1,\qquad\theta=\frac{2d}a,\qquad\eta=\eta_d=\min\Bigl\{\frac15,\frac1a\Bigr\},
6	\]
7	and $\eps$ with $0<\eps<\eta/2$ is fixed. We put $\eps_1=\eps/2$ and apply \cref{prop:reduction,prop:initial} with $\eps_1$ in place of $\eps$. Constants written $C_f$ depend only on $f$, constants written $C_{f,\eps}$ depend only on $f$ and $\eps$, and both may change from line to line. (Archived source: proposition P7.)
8	
9	\section{The variance on an interval of moduli}
10	
11	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:interval}
12	Let $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$, $2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$ and $2\le R\le x$, and let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)$ be as in \cref{prop:averaging}. Then
13	\[
14	\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A\bigr).
15	\]
16	\end{lemma}
17	
18	\begin{proof}
19	\emph{Correlations.} For $z<k\le y$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ integers $h$ with $1\le h\le x/f(k)$, and each $m=hf(k)$ is an integer in $[1,x]$. By \cref{prop:corr}, replacing $C_x(m)$ by $(x-m)\Sing(m)$ costs at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{4/5}$ for each pair $(h,k)$. After multiplying by $f'(k)$ and summing over $h$, the cost is at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}f'(k)/f(k)$, and by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
20	\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-M}
21	|S_f(x;z,y)-M_f(x;z,y)|\le2UK_{\mathrm c}\,x^{9/5}\log(2x).
22	\end{equation}
23	\emph{Averaging.} \Cref{prop:averaging} applies under exactly the present hypotheses and gives
24	\[
25	|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2\mathcal A,\qquad|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_f\mathcal A,
26	\]
27	where we used $\widetilde R_f=R_f$ (\cref{prop:Df}(d)).
28	
29	\emph{Combination.} By \cref{prop:reduction}, the factor $2$ in front of $S_f$ and the factor $x^2$ in front of $T_f$ give
30	\begin{multline*}
31	\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-\bigl[cx(Y-Z)+2I_f(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr]\Bigr|\\
32	\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}\bigr)+4UK_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}\log(2x)+3C_fx^2\mathcal A.
33	\end{multline*}
34	\emph{Exact cancellation.} By \cref{lem:integral-identity}, $2I_f(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)$. By the definition \eqref{eq:ThetaF} of $F_f$, with $c=\zeta(2)^{-1}$, direct subtraction gives
35	\[
36	x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)=-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y),
37	\]
38	because $x^2\cdot c/(x/Y)=cxY$ and the $B_f$-terms cancel. Hence the bracket equals $x^2(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z))$.
39	\end{proof}
40	
41	\section{Choice of the cutoffs and the error budget}\label{sec:budget}
42	
43	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:main1}]
44	Take
45	\[
46	Z=x^\theta=x^{2d/a},\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
47	\]
48	Both exponents lie in $(0,1)$. Choose $x_0=x_0(f)\ge2$ so that $Z\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}$ and $R\ge2$ for $x\ge x_0$; then also $Z\le x$ and $R\le x$. By \cref{lem:poly}(a) there is a unique real $z\ge1$ with $f(z)=Z$. Then
49	\begin{equation}\label{eq:exponents}
50	\begin{gathered}
51	Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a},\qquad1+\theta\Bigl(2-\frac1d\Bigr)=\frac{8d-3}a=2-\frac1a,\\
52	\Bigl(2-\frac1a\Bigr)-\Bigl(\frac12+\frac{3d}a\Bigr)=\frac{6d-5}{2a}>0.
53	\end{gathered}
54	\end{equation}
55	
56	\emph{Case $Y\ge Z$.} Then $z\le y$, and $V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y)$. Hence
57	\[
58	|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|\le V_f(x,z)+x^2|F_f(x/Z)|+\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|.
59	\]
60	We bound every term; the table summarises the result.
61	\begin{itemize}
62	\item By \cref{prop:initial} and \eqref{eq:exponents}, $V_f(x,z)\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Z^{2-1/d}=C_{f,\eps}x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}$.
63	\item By \eqref{eq:F-asym} with $H=x/Z\ge1$, $x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}\le C_fx^{2-1/a}$, by \eqref{eq:exponents}.
64	\item By \cref{lem:interval} the remaining difference is at most $C_{f,\eps}$ times $x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A$, and by \eqref{eq:exponents} and $R\le x$, $x^2\mathcal A\le x^{2-1/a}\bigl((\log2x)^2+(\log2x)^3\bigr)$.
65	\end{itemize}
66	\begin{center}
67	\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
68	\toprule
69	origin & bound & comparison with $x^{2-\eta+\eps}$\\
70	\midrule
71	diagonal and mixed terms (\cref{prop:reduction}) & $x^{3/2+\eps_1}$ & $\eta\le\frac15<\frac12$\\
72	endpoint of $\sum f'(k)$ (\cref{prop:reduction}) & $xY^{1-1/d}\le x^{2-1/d}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a\le\frac1d$\\
73	correlations (\cref{prop:corr}) & $x^{9/5}\log(2x)$ & $\eta\le\frac15$, $\log2x\ll_\eps x^{\eps}$\\
74	averaging (\cref{prop:averaging}) & $x^{2-1/a}(\log2x)^3$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$, $(\log2x)^3\ll_\eps x^{\eps}$\\
75	initial moduli (\cref{prop:initial}) & $x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$\\
76	lower boundary of the profile & $x^{1/2+3d/a}\le x^{2-1/a}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$\\
77	\bottomrule
78	\end{tabular}
79	\end{center}
80	The logarithmic bounds come from \cref{lem:sums}(d). Every row is at most $C_{f,\eps}x^{2-\eta+\eps}$ for $x\ge2$, which proves \eqref{eq:main1} when $Y\ge Z$.
81	
82	\emph{Case $Y<Z$.} Apply \cref{prop:initial} with $y$ in place of $z$; this is allowed since $y\ge1$ and $f(y)=Y\le x$. Because $2-1/d>0$,
83	\[
84	0\le V_f(x,y)\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Y^{2-1/d}\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Z^{2-1/d}=C_{f,\eps}x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}.
85	\]
86	Also $x/Y\ge1$, so \eqref{eq:F-asym} and \eqref{eq:exponents} give $x^2|F_f(x/Y)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\le C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}\le C_fx^{2-1/a}$. The triangle inequality and $\eta\le1/a$ give \eqref{eq:main1} in this case too.
87	
88	All constants and $x_0$ depend only on $f$ and $\eps$, and real values of $y$ and $z$ need no separate treatment: the sums split exactly as $k\le z$ and $z<k\le y$, and the endpoint effects are contained in \cref{prop:reduction}.
89	\end{proof}
90	
91	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:main2}]
92	For every $Y\le x$, \eqref{eq:F-asym} with $H=x/Y\ge1$, multiplied by $x^2$, gives
93	\[
94	\bigl|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\bigr|\le C_fx^2(x/Y)^{-13/8}=C_fx^{3/8}Y^{13/8},
95	\]
96	since $x^2(x/Y)^{-3/2}=x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$. Combine this with \eqref{eq:main1}. The formulas \eqref{eq:K-intro} and \eqref{eq:R-intro} and the positivity of $K_f$ are \cref{prop:Df}(d),(f).
97	\end{proof}
98	
99	\begin{remark}
100	The archived assembly notes that the hypothesis $\eps<\eta_d/2$ is not used: the argument works for every $\eps>0$. We keep the hypothesis as stated.
101	\end{remark}
102	
103	\section{Proof of \cref{cor:range}}\label{sec:corollary}
104	
105	Let $0<\delta<\eta/3$, apply \eqref{eq:main2} with $\eps=\delta$ (admissible because $\delta<\eta/2$), and divide by $K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$, which is positive by \cref{prop:Df}(f). For $x^{1-2\eta/3+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ the two relative errors are
106	\[
107	\frac{x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}}=\Bigl(\frac Yx\Bigr)^{1/8}\le x^{-\delta/8},\qquad
108	\frac{x^{2-\eta+\delta}}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}}\le x^{3/2-\eta+\delta-\frac32(1-\frac{2\eta}3+\delta)}=x^{-\delta/2}\le x^{-\delta/8}.
109	\]
110	Hence $|V_f(x,y)/(K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2})-1|\le C(f,\delta)x^{-\delta/8}$ for $x\ge x_0(f,\delta)$. The range is nonempty because $\delta<\eta/3$. This deduction is carried out in both archived integration reports, one of them with $\eps=\delta/2$; it is not part of an approved proposition (see \texttt{changes.md}). \qed
111	
112	\section{Where the exponents come from}
113	
114	The cap $\eta_d\le\frac15$ comes from summing the uniform correlation error $x^{4/5}$ of \cref{prop:corr} over all pairs $(h,k)$; the weighted number of these pairs is $\sum_kf'(k)x/f(k)\asymp x\log x$. \chapter{Proof of the main theorem}\label{ch:assembly}

We now combine \cref{prop:reduction,prop:initial,prop:corr,prop:averaging,prop:Df,prop:Theta} and \cref{lem:integral-identity}. Throughout, $d=\deg f$,
\[
a=4d-1,\qquad\theta=\frac{2d}a,\qquad\eta=\eta_d=\min\Bigl\{\frac15,\frac1a\Bigr\},
\]
and $\eps$ with $0<\eps<\eta/2$ is fixed. We put $\eps_1=\eps/2$ and apply \cref{prop:reduction,prop:initial} with $\eps_1$ in place of $\eps$. Constants written $C_f$ depend only on $f$, constants written $C_{f,\eps}$ depend only on $f$ and $\eps$, and both may change from line to line. (Archived source: proposition P7.)

\section{The variance on an interval of moduli}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:interval}
Let $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$, $2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$ and $2\le R\le x$, and let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)$ be as in \cref{prop:averaging}. Then
\[
\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Correlations.} For $z<k\le y$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ integers $h$ with $1\le h\le x/f(k)$, and each $m=hf(k)$ is an integer in $[1,x]$. By \cref{prop:corr}, replacing $C_x(m)$ by $(x-m)\Sing(m)$ costs at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{4/5}$ for each pair $(h,k)$. After multiplying by $f'(k)$ and summing over $h$, the cost is at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}f'(k)/f(k)$, and by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-M}
|S_f(x;z,y)-M_f(x;z,y)|\le2UK_{\mathrm c}\,x^{9/5}\log(2x).
\end{equation}
\emph{Averaging.} \Cref{prop:averaging} applies under exactly the present hypotheses and gives
\[
|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2\mathcal A,\qquad|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_f\mathcal A,
\]
where we used $\widetilde R_f=R_f$ (\cref{prop:Df}(d)).

\emph{Combination.} By \cref{prop:reduction}, the factor $2$ in front of $S_f$ and the factor $x^2$ in front of $T_f$ give
\begin{multline*}
\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-\bigl[cx(Y-Z)+2I_f(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr]\Bigr|\\
\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}\bigr)+4UK_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}\log(2x)+3C_fx^2\mathcal A.
\end{multline*}
\emph{Exact cancellation.} By \cref{lem:integral-identity}, $2I_f(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)$. By the definition \eqref{eq:ThetaF} of $F_f$, with $c=\zeta(2)^{-1}$, direct subtraction gives
\[
x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)=-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y),
\]
because $x^2\cdot c/(x/Y)=cxY$ and the $B_f$-terms cancel. Hence the bracket equals $x^2(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z))$.
\end{proof}

\section{Choice of the cutoffs and the error budget}\label{sec:budget}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:main1}]
Take
\[
Z=x^\theta=x^{2d/a},\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
\]
Both exponents lie in $(0,1)$. Choose $x_0=x_0(f)\ge2$ so that $Z\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}$ and $R\ge2$ for $x\ge x_0$; then also $Z\le x$ and $R\le x$. By \cref{lem:poly}(a) there is a unique real $z\ge1$ with $f(z)=Z$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exponents}
\begin{gathered}
Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a},\qquad1+\theta\Bigl(2-\frac1d\Bigr)=\frac{8d-3}a=2-\frac1a,\\
\Bigl(2-\frac1a\Bigr)-\Bigl(\frac12+\frac{3d}a\Bigr)=\frac{6d-5}{2a}>0.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

\emph{Case $Y\ge Z$.} Then $z\le y$, and $V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y)$. Hence
\[
|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|\le V_f(x,z)+x^2|F_f(x/Z)|+\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|.
\]
We bound every term; the table summarises the result.
\begin{itemize}
\item By \cref{prop:initial} and \eqref{eq:exponents}, $V_f(x,z)\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Z^{2-1/d}=C_{f,\eps}x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}$.
\item By \eqref{eq:F-asym} with $H=x/Z\ge1$, $x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}\le C_fx^{2-1/a}$, by \eqref{eq:exponents}.
\item By \cref{lem:interval} the remaining difference is at most $C_{f,\eps}$ times $x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A$, and by \eqref{eq:exponents} and $R\le x$, $x^2\mathcal A\le x^{2-1/a}\bigl((\log2x)^2+(\log2x)^3\bigr)$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
origin & bound & comparison with $x^{2-\eta+\eps}$\\
\midrule
diagonal and mixed terms (\cref{prop:reduction}) & $x^{3/2+\eps_1}$ & $\eta\le\frac15<\frac12$\\
endpoint of $\sum f'(k)$ (\cref{prop:reduction}) & $xY^{1-1/d}\le x^{2-1/d}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a\le\frac1d$\\
correlations (\cref{prop:corr}) & $x^{9/5}\log(2x)$ & $\eta\le\frac15$, $\log2x\ll_\eps x^{\eps}$\\
averaging (\cref{prop:averaging}) & $x^{2-1/a}(\log2x)^3$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$, $(\log2x)^3\ll_\eps x^{\eps}$\\
initial moduli (\cref{prop:initial}) & $x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$\\
lower boundary of the profile & $x^{1/2+3d/a}\le x^{2-1/a}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The logarithmic bounds come from \cref{lem:sums}(d). Every row is at most $C_{f,\eps}x^{2-\eta+\eps}$ for $x\ge2$, which proves \eqref{eq:main1} when $Y\ge Z$.

\emph{Case $Y<Z$.} Apply \cref{prop:initial} with $y$ in place of $z$; this is allowed since $y\ge1$ and $f(y)=Y\le x$. Because $2-1/d>0$,
\[
0\le V_f(x,y)\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Y^{2-1/d}\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Z^{2-1/d}=C_{f,\eps}x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}.
\]
Also $x/Y\ge1$, so \eqref{eq:F-asym} and \eqref{eq:exponents} give $x^2|F_f(x/Y)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\le C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}\le C_fx^{2-1/a}$. The triangle inequality and $\eta\le1/a$ give \eqref{eq:main1} in this case too.

All constants and $x_0$ depend only on $f$ and $\eps$, and real values of $y$ and $z$ need no separate treatment: the sums split exactly as $k\le z$ and $z<k\le y$, and the endpoint effects are contained in \cref{prop:reduction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:main2}]
For every $Y\le x$, \eqref{eq:F-asym} with $H=x/Y\ge1$, multiplied by $x^2$, gives
\[
\bigl|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\bigr|\le C_fx^2(x/Y)^{-13/8}=C_fx^{3/8}Y^{13/8},
\]
since $x^2(x/Y)^{-3/2}=x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$. Combine this with \eqref{eq:main1}. The formulas \eqref{eq:K-intro} and \eqref{eq:R-intro} and the positivity of $K_f$ are \cref{prop:Df}(d),(f).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The archived assembly notes that the hypothesis $\eps<\eta_d/2$ is not used: the argument works for every $\eps>0$. We keep the hypothesis as stated.
\end{remark}

\section{Proof of \cref{cor:range}}\label{sec:corollary}

Let $0<\delta<\eta/3$, apply \eqref{eq:main2} with $\eps=\delta$ (admissible because $\delta<\eta/2$), and divide by $K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$, which is positive by \cref{prop:Df}(f). For $x^{1-2\eta/3+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ the two relative errors are
\[
\frac{x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}}=\Bigl(\frac Yx\Bigr)^{1/8}\le x^{-\delta/8},\qquad
\frac{x^{2-\eta+\delta}}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}}\le x^{3/2-\eta+\delta-\frac32(1-\frac{2\eta}3+\delta)}=x^{-\delta/2}\le x^{-\delta/8}.
\]
Hence $|V_f(x,y)/(K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2})-1|\le C(f,\delta)x^{-\delta/8}$ for $x\ge x_0(f,\delta)$. The range is nonempty because $\delta<\eta/3$. This deduction is carried out in both archived integration reports, one of them with $\eps=\delta/2$; it is not part of an approved proposition (see \texttt{changes.md}). \qed

\section{Where the exponents come from}

The cap $\eta_d\le\frac15$ comes from summing the uniform correlation error $x^{4/5}$ of \cref{prop:corr} over all pairs $(h,k)$; the weighted number of these pairs is $\sum_kf'(k)x/f(k)\asymp x\log x$. The exponent $\frac1{4d-1}$ comes from balancing two terms. The first is the bound $x^{1+\eps}Z^{2-1/d}$ for the initial moduli; it arises from multiplying the full-variance bound \eqref{eq:full-variance} by the largest weight $f'(k)\asymp Z^{1-1/d}$. The second is the averaging error $x^2Z^{-1/(2d)}$ of \cref{prop:averaging} at $R=Z^{1/d}$. Equating $1+\theta(2-\frac1d)$ with $2-\frac\theta{2d}$ gives $\theta=\frac{2d}{4d-1}$. Improving either the treatment of small moduli or the correlation estimate would widen the range of \cref{cor:range}. Neither improvement is attempted here.
